presentations.presentation_title: Dispersive Out-of-ecliptic Solar Particle Events Observed by Epd on Solar Orbiter
presentations.abstract: With its inclined orbit, Solar Orbiter now reaches higher heliocentric latitudes than are accessible from the ecliptic. We will investigate small, dispersive solar particle events and compare their onset times with X-ray measurements. Using the first particles to arrive, we determine the path lengths along which they traveled and compare these with the expected values. This exploratory work could help elucidate the global configuration of the coronal and interplanetary magnetic field and discern between traditional models and, e.g., the Fisk model.

presentations.presentation_title: Cosmic-ray Modulation Over One Solar Cycle Observed by CALET on the International Space Station
presentations.institution: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: The CALorimetric Electron Telescope (CALET), installed on the International Space Station (ISS), has been observing high-energy cosmic rays (CRs) and gamma rays since October 2015 to investigate the acceleration and propagation of cosmic rays. In addition to the high-energy (HE) trigger with an energy threshold of approximately 10 GeV, CALET adopts a low-energy electron (LEE) trigger operating at high geomagnetic latitudes, which enables measurements of low-energy cosmic rays in the energy range from 1 to 10 GeV. Using this LEE trigger, CALET has continuously observed the solar modulation of low-energy electrons and protons over nearly one full solar cycle. During an observation period spanning the late solar cycle 24 through the ongoing solar cycle 25, CALET has detected a charge-sign dependence of the cosmic-ray modulation consistent with numerical drift models of the low-energy CR transport in the heliosphere. In addition, CALET has successfully detected several Forbush decreases, including those that occurred in May 2024, in agreement with ground-based neutron monitor observations. In this presentation, we report a comprehensive overview of the solar modulation of low-energy electrons and protons observed by CALET. We also discuss the charge-sign dependence observed in both the long-term modulation associated with solar activity and short-term variations, such as Forbush decreases.

presentations.presentation_title: Solar Energetic Electron Events on 2022 December 24
presentations.abstract: We investigate two adjacent solar energetic electron (SEE) events measured by Solar Orbiter/EPD at 0.93 au with a separation of ~30 minutes on December 24, 2022. STEREO-A (Wind) with a longitudinal separation of ~5° (19°) from Solar Orbiter shows no clear observations of SEEs, indicating the presence of a <20° longitudinal distribution for these two events. In addition, the nearly symmetric peaks in temporal profiles and strongly beamed pitch angle distributions in both events suggest that most of these SEEs undergo essentially scatter-free propagation in the interplanetary medium. Utilizing the pan-spectrum fitting method, we self-consistently determine the spectral shape of background-subtracted electron peak flux vs energy. Event #1 is fitted to a triple power-law spectrum with two spectral breaks at ~22 and 290 keV. Event #2 shows a double power-law spectrum with a spectral break around 25 keV. For both events, the power-law spectrum extends down to below 10 keV, implying that these SEEs could originate high in the corona. We further derive the electron injection profiles at sun by forward fitting in-situ temporal profiles, for the two events. According to the characteristics of injection timing and spectral shape, Event #1 consists of three SEE populations, respectively, at energies below ~22 keV, between ~22 keV and ~290 keV, and above ~290 keV, while Event #2 consists of two populations, respectively, at energies below and above ~25 keV. The low-energy population likely provides seed populations for further acceleration process (processes) to form the high-energy population (populations).

presentations.presentation_title: Impulsive Solar Energetic Particle Events at High Heliolatitude
presentations.institution: Macau University of Science and Technology
presentations.abstract: We present observations of impulsive solar energetic particle (SEP) events on 2025 March 20 at high heliolatitudes by Solar Orbiter and compare them with in-ecliptic observations by the Wind spacecraft. Solar Orbiter, located at 0.38 au, a Carrington longitude of 139.7◦ and a latitude of −16.6◦, observed two ion events at ∼0.1-6 MeV and two electron events at ∼40-200 keV exhibiting clear velocity dispersion and strong field-aligned anisotropy. VDA of both ion and electron events yields path lengths consistent with the nominal Parker spiral length. Moreover, the first electron event exhibits a double-power-law spectrum with an index of 2.3 ± 0.3 below a break energy of 58 ± 4 keV and an index of 4.0 ± 0.2 at energies above, while the second electron event exhibits a single-power-law spectrum with an index of 4.6 ± 0.2. In contrast, the Wind spacecraft, located at 1 au, a Carrington longitude of 120.0◦, and a latitude of −7.1◦, observed only one electron event, which shows insignificant velocity dispersion and arrives ∼20 min later than expected. These results suggest that impulsive SEP events can extend over at least ∼10° in latitude and ∼15° in longitude in the interplanetary medium, while their angular separation from the source region may reach ∼30° in latitude and ∼50° in longitude. Furthermore, electron-only SEP events observed at 1 au may have their proton counterparts close to the Sun.

presentations.presentation_title: Relationship between Microwave Peak Flux/Fluence and Soft X-ray Peak Flux in Solar Flares
presentations.abstract: In general, large solar flares in GOES soft X-ray (SXR) class show relatively intense emissions in other wavelengths, such as radio, hard X-rays, and so forth. SXRs are mainly emitted by thermal plasma in coronal flaring loops. On the other hand, microwaves are mainly emitted by non-thermal accelerated electrons moving in the flaring loops. Even though their emission processes are different, Kawate et al. (2011) compared the peak flux in 17 GHz and GOES SXR peak flux for more than 800 flares observed with Nobeyama Radiheliograph and found there is a positive correlation between them with a correlation coefficient of about 0.6. This means electron acceleration process is closely related with plasma heating process in solar flares. This correlation is useful for some applications. Matsumoto et al. (2023) independently derived the correlation in peak flux between microwaves and GOES SXRs and estimated the GOES X-ray classes for two quite intense solar flares in 1956 (before starting GOES observations) from the old microwave observational records. Thus, it is important to derive an accurate relationship between microwaves and SXRs not only for the understanding of the electron acceleration process in the whole scenario of solar flare but also this kind of study. Here, it is known that the time integral of nonthermal emissions corresponds well to the rise phase of thermal emissions (Neupert 1968). However, most of previous studies did not use time integral (fluence) for microwaves. Thus, we analyzed the microwave data taken by Nobeyama Radio Polarimeters and compared the microwave fluences and GOES SXR peak flux. The result indicated that the correlation coefficient does not become significantly better compared with the results of the previous studies. We discuss this result from several points of view, such as analysis method, data quality, emission process and so on.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Properties of EMIC Waves in Multi-ion Plasmas: Insights from Full-wave Simulations
presentations.abstract: Electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves play a crucial role in Earth's magnetosphere-ionosphere by actively interacting with both electrons and ions. Recent advances in satellite observations have significantly improved our understanding of EMIC wave properties; however, satellite measurements are limited in their ability to track wave characteristics along their entire propagation paths. The presence of heavier ions, such as He + and O + , can influence wave propagation, leading to distinct bands of EMIC waves, such as H + -, He + -, and O + -band EMIC waves. The heavier ions also affect wave propagation by introducing additional cutoffs, resonances, and crossovers. However, the lack of global simulations has hindered our understanding of EMIC wave propagation from the source (e.g., the magnetic equator) to the ground in multi-ion magnetospheric plasmas. Recent full-wave simulations of EMIC waves have successfully demonstrated their propagation and provided new insights into their properties, including polarization, wave-normal angle, and transmission coefficient into the ionosphere. In this presentation, we review the full-wave simulations of EMIC waves in the inner and outer magnetosphere and compare the results with observations from the Van Allen Probes, Cluster, MMS, and Arase satellites.

presentations.presentation_title: Investigating the Effects and Propagation Efficiency of Lightning-Generated Whistlers from Arase and WWLLN Data
presentations.abstract: Lightning discharges in Earth’s atmosphere emit electromagnetic waves across a broad frequency spectrum. In the very low frequency range, part of this energy propagates upward into the ionosphere and leaks into the inner magnetosphere as whistler-mode waves. These lightning-generated whistlers (LGW) can pitch-angle scatter radiation-belt electrons, leading to their precipitation into the atmosphere. Numerous previous studies have suggested that lightning plays a significant role in radiation belt electron losses, including in the creation and persistence of the slot region. However, a year-long comparison between global lightning activity by the World Wide Lightning Location Network (WWLLN) and trapped electron fluxes observed by the Van Allen Probes (RBSP) revealed a significantly weaker effect than theoretically expected [Martinez-Calderon+(2020)]. A more recent analysis using similar methodology, but now combining WWLLN, RBSP, and Arase observations for 2018, has found similar low correlation. We suggest that ducted LGW propagate to the radiation belts with low efficiency despite their effectiveness in driving pitch-angle scattering. We focused on periods of intense lightning activity in 2018, where we identified whistler events detected by Arase. We then performed a polarization analysis and selected ducted LGW (wave-normal angles <32° [Wold+(2024)]) and estimated the fraction of ducted whistlers using a semi-automated detection algorithm (based on Oike+(2014)). Preliminary results suggest that the fraction of ducted whistlers among all observed whistlers is about 9%. Comparing with lightning activity during the same time interval and within the corresponding spatial region, we estimate that only ~4% of original spherics penetrated through the ionosphere and continued propagating as ducted whistlers into the inner magnetosphere. This suggests a low whistler propagation efficiency, explaining the low correlations with trapped flux observations. We will discuss these results, as well as the limitations of our current semi-automated detection system and possibilities for improvement.

presentations.presentation_title: Evolution of NWC Transmitter Wave Power Distribution from the Topside Ionosphere Into the Inner Magnetosphere
presentations.institution: The University of Texas at Dallas
presentations.abstract: Ground-based VLF transmitters emit signals that primarily propagate within the Earth–ionosphere waveguide, and some of their energy can propagate into the magnetosphere. Ionospheric observations from the DEMETER satellite reveal a distinct concentric ring pattern of the wave power distribution of the NWC transmitter in the transverse (longitude–L-shell) plane. Using data from the Van Allen Probes and Arase/ERG satellites, we find that the concentric rings pattern is still visible but becomes less distinct. The pattern shifts outward, and becomes more elliptic as the wave propagates from the southern ionosphere to the Northern Hemisphere. To investigate the cause of this evolution, we performed ray tracing simulations under three conditions: (1) ducted propagation; (2) non-ducted propagation with vertical initial wave normal angles; and (3) non-ducted propagation with spread initial wave normal angles. The results show that non-ducted propagation with spread wave normal angles best explains the observed evolution of wave power distribution pattern during the propagation.

presentations.presentation_title: Inner Radiation Belt Simulations During the Major Space Weather Event of May 2024
presentations.institution: International Research Center for Space and Planetary Environmental Science (i-SPES), Kyushu University
presentations.abstract: While observational studies have reported proton flux enhancement at L=1.6-2.2 in the inner belt during the major space weather event of May 2024, its detailed dynamics remain poorly understood due to the limited observational capabilities of spacecraft missions. Therefore, we performed large-scale test particle simulations to investigate the spatio-temporal evolution of the proton inner belt. The time-dependent electromagnetic field was produced using the Tsyganenko and IGRF models, including the corresponding inductive electric field. Our results successfully reproduced the observed proton flux enhancement in the inner belt. Furthermore, the overall proton belt dynamics were found to be energy-dependent, influenced by the evolving electromagnetic fields. Finally, we conclude that the dominant driver of the inner belt dynamics was the reconfiguration of the background field during the magnetic storm more than the Solar Proton Event impact.

presentations.presentation_title: Transient Distortions of the South Atlantic Anomaly Radiation Environments Driven by Large-scale Electric Fields
presentations.abstract: Energetic electrons in Earth's inner radiation belt pose significant hazards to spacecraft systems, with the strongest radiation in low-Earth orbit (LEO) mostly confined to the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA) region. Once considered stable, the inner belt is now understood to exhibit significant variability. Using data from the low-Earth-orbit Macau Science Satellite-1 mission, we report transient distortions of the SAA radiation environments, observationally characterized by enhanced fluxes of energetic electrons outside the traditional SAA region, appearing either attached to or detached from the boundary. We show that these distortions are induced by large-scale electric-field perturbations that adiabatically alter the electron mirror heights, which can be further modulated by ultra-low-frequency waves. Test-particle simulations successfully reproduce the observational features and provide new constraints on the properties of the associated electric fields. These findings reveal a distinct manifestation of inner belt variability, extending the electron radiation risks beyond the expected SAA boundaries.

presentations.presentation_title: Quiet-time Suprathermal Intensities and Composition Observed by Solar Orbiter
presentations.abstract: The joint ESA/NASA Solar Orbiter mission has observed suprathermal and energetic particles throughout much of Solar Cycle 25, spanning the period from 2020 to 2025, providing unprecedented coverage of the inner heliosphere. Measurements of protons, and heavy ions show substantial temporal variability in particle intensities over the solar cycle. In particular, the Suprathermal Ion Spectrograph (SIS) of the Solar Orbiter Energetic Particle Detector (EPD) measures suprathermal ion abundances from hydrogen through iron with high precision. Previous studies have shown that the suprathermal ion population in the heliosphere arises from multiple source populations. In this work, we focus on the composition and origin of the quiet-time suprathermal population, using Solar Orbiter/SIS composition measurements to examine how source contributions vary with solar activity level and heliocentric distance. We find that during periods of low solar activity and relatively stable particle intensities, the suprathermal heavy-ion composition closely resembles that of the ambient solar wind and/or corotating interaction regions, indicating that these sources make a dominant contribution under quiet conditions. Impulsive material, such as 3 He-rich ions, becomes more prominent during more active intervals but represents a reduced fraction of the suprathermal pool during quiet times. These observations demonstrate that the quiet-time suprathermal population in the inner heliosphere is largely controlled by solar-related sources, providing important constraints on the seed population available for subsequent energetic particle acceleration.

presentations.presentation_title: Proton and Heavy Ion Acceleration by Magnetic Reconnection at the Near-sun Heliospheric Current Sheet
presentations.abstract: Magnetic reconnection at the near-Sun heliospheric current sheet (HCS) dissipates the Parker spiral and converts magnetic energy into plasma kinetic energy. During Encounter 14 (E14) at a radial distance of ∼16.25 R ⊙ ​, Parker Solar Probe (PSP) observed an HCS crossing where reconnection-driven acceleration—likely facilitated by merging large-scale flux tubes—energized protons up to ∼400 keV. This energy gain is ≈1000 times greater than the available magnetic energy per particle. We present here a comprehensive analysis of pitch-angle distributions and differential energy spectra for protons and heavy ions (He, O, and Fe) in conjunction with local wave activity during this crossing. Our results provide the first direct in situ observations of simultaneous proton and heavy-ion energization during HCS reconnection. Crucially, we find that heavy-ion power-law spectral indices differ significantly from those of protons, contradicting previous simulations that predict species-independent slopes. We further demonstrate that ion beams and anisotropies produced during reconnection drive waves in the ion cyclotron range of frequencies. Finally, we show that proton pitch-angle scattering is stronger than that of heavy ions, which may account for the flatter spectra or harder spectral indices observed in the heavy-ion populations. These observations provide definitive evidence for in situ reconnection-driven acceleration at the near-Sun HCS and necessitate the inclusion of species-dependent transport and acceleration efficiencies in contemporary reconnection-based particle energization models.

presentations.presentation_title: Upstream Ion Events Revisited: IMAP/CoDICE observations
presentations.abstract: Ion intensity enhancements extending up to ~1 MeV/nucleon originating from the vicinity of the Earth are observed in the upstream interplanetary space and are known as upstream ion events. Despite the abundance of data in the past, it remains still unclear which fraction of these ions is accelerated at the bow shock or inside the Earth’s magnetosphere. The Compact Dual Ion Composition Experiment (CoDICE) on the Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) measures charge states of suprathermal ions (<80 keV/q) in nearly all sky coverage, enabling the charge state analysis of the Earth originated ions at 1 AU for the first time. This advantage provides clear separation of solar-wind ions/suprathermals from plasmas of terrestrial origin. Focusing on the charge-state distributions in this energy range and mass distribution of the energetic ions, we will discuss the source of the newly identified events and compare with past observations. IMAP was launched in September 2025, and CODICE comprises one of the in-situ instrument suite. CoDICE combines an electrostatic analyzer (ESA) with a common time-of-flight (TOF) versus energy (TOF/E) subsystem to simultaneously measure the 3D velocity distribution functions and ionic charge state and mass composition of 0.5–80 keV/q ions in the lower-energy section (CoDICE-Lo), and the mass composition and sectored arrival velocity of 0.03–5 MeV/n ions in the high-er energy section (CoDICE-Hi). CoDICE is comprised of two major subsystems: ESA subsystem, and a shared TOF/E subsystem. The high-energy sensor head (CoDICE-Hi) has a separate entrance aperture for detecting energetic ions. The shared design optimizes the resource, and the usage of Avalanche Photodiodes (APD) reduces the post acceleration voltage to -15 kV.

presentations.presentation_title: Proton Acceleration During the Interaction of a Cme-driven Shock and Current Sheet
presentations.abstract: The shock geometry is crucial to the acceleration efficiency of energetic particles. It is essential to study particle behavior under different shock geometry while maintaining comparable shock properties such as strength, speed, and turbulence conditions within a continuous period of time. In this work, we study the physical process of the interaction between an interplanetary shock and current sheet, and compare the energetic protons behaviors under different shock geometries separated by a current sheet using the Electron-Proton Telescope on board the Solar Orbiter (SolO) on 2023 March. We find that the current sheet is possibly related to a magnetic reconnection whose exhaust region extends to the shock. The differential flux of 60 keV - 2 MeV protons enhances by 2.5 times from the current sheet until the shock. During the quasi-parallel shock interval, the first-order flux anisotropy in the plasma frame is consistent with the diffusive shock acceleration. Nevertheless, the flux anisotropy exhibits a bipolar shape during the quasi-perpendicular shock interval. The coexistence of positive and negative flux anisotropy suggests that the magnetic field is wandering around the shock and connected to the shock surface with different acceleration efficiency. The flux anisotropy peaks at the transition energy indicates that it is influenced by the current sheet. The break energy is greater during the quasi-perpendicular interval, implying a more efficient proton acceleration. We suggest that the current sheet is an important ingredient that affects the local shock geometry, and thus the particle acceleration efficiency and flux anisotropy. This effect can be accumulated as the shock traveling outward from the Sun and may need consideration in explaining the observed particle spectra profiles at further distances.

presentations.presentation_title: Self-generation of Whistler Waves and Nonthermal Electron Acceleration at Earth’s Bow Shock
presentations.abstract: The acceleration of charged particles at collisionless shocks has attracted considerable attention in the plasma physics community. Bright radio and X-ray synchrotron emissions from strong astrophysical shocks provide compelling evidence for the production of ultra-relativistic electrons in these environments. In contrast, enhancements of nonthermal electrons associated with shocks are relatively rare in heliospheric observations. This observational discrepancy may be related to the so-called electron injection problem, namely, our limited understanding of the efficiency of electron pre-acceleration to the threshold energy required for participation in standard diffusive shock acceleration. Stochastic shock drift acceleration (SSDA) has been proposed as a promising mechanism for electron injection at shocks and has been shown to reproduce key characteristics of nonthermal electrons observed by spacecraft at Earth’s bow shock. However, efficient SSDA requires intense wave activity in the shock transition region to provide sufficient scattering and confinement of accelerated electrons, and the underlying wave generation mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigate the origin of such waves and their dependence on macroscopic shock parameters, focusing on high-frequency whistler-mode waves as a candidate scattering agent. Using a statistical analysis of Earth’s bow shock observations by the MMS spacecraft, we find that the wave power increases with increasing Alfven Mach number in the de Hoffmann-Teller frame. We show that this trend can be explained by instabilities driven by electrons reflected through adiabatic shock drift acceleration (SDA). Once wave generation is triggered, the reflected electrons can be scattered and effectively confined within the shock, thereby transforming SDA into SSDA. We argue that this self-generation scenario provides a natural explanation for the realization of SSDA and is consistent with existing observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Acceleration of Radiation Belt Electrons via Ultra-Low Frequency Waves Generated by a Foreshock Transient
presentations.abstract: Radiation belt electrons can be energized by ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves through resonant wave-particle interactions. Foreshock transients, which are mesoscale structures upstream of the Earth’s bow shock, can generate ULF waves when they impact the magnetosphere. Foreshock transients evolve from solar wind discontinuities in the foreshock region, and they are commonly observed. However, their effect on radiation belt dynamics has not been studied before. We present a case study of a foreshock transient event that is associated with localized ULF wave activity and prompt acceleration in electron fluxes, utilizing multi-satellite observations. The transient is characterized by hot and tenuous plasma, strong flow deflection and is bounded by a compressed edge on its sunward side indicating that it is a foreshock bubble. Using data from Arase, Van Allen Probes and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites that were all favorably located during this event, we can assess the global view of the transient’s effects on the dayside inner magnetosphere. The electron fluxes from these satellites show signatures of an initial energization and subsequent drift echoes. This injection exhibits energy dispersion and boomerang stripes in the pitch angle distributions. Analysis of energy and pitch angle dependent drift speeds shows that the acceleration is consistent with the timing and geometry of the impact of the foreshock bubble. Wave measurements from these spacecraft similarly show enhanced ULF wave activity at the time of the bubble impact and the electron injection. This study shows, for the first time, that foreshock transients can energize radiation belt electrons via ULF waves. Thus, they may play an important role in radiation belt dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Statistical Features of ELF/VLF Plasma Wave Spectra in the Inner Magnetosphere Derived from the Long-term Arase Satellite Observation
presentations.abstract: We report average plasma wave spectra in the ELF/VLF range in the inner magnetosphere derived from long-term observations achieved by the Arase satellite. The Arase satellite has provided high-quality datasets for over 9 years since its launch in 2016. The highly inclined elliptical satellite orbit enables investigation of the particle and plasma wave environments in the inner magnetosphere over a wide L-shell and magnetic latitude range, which has been quite difficult for previous satellite missions to accomplish. The Plasma Wave Experiment (PWE) onboard the Arase satellite is designed to measure electromagnetic fields in the frequency range from DC to 10 MHz for the electric field and from a few Hz to 100 kHz for the magnetic field. The Onboard Frequency Analyzer (OFA), which is part of PWE, processes electromagnetic fields over the frequency range from 64 Hz to 20 kHz and provides frequency spectra and spectral matrices of the electric and magnetic fields. In this study, we statistically analyze data from OFA to determine average plasma wave frequency spectra in the ELF/VLF range in the inner magnetosphere. It is important to determine the statistical properties of waves in that frequency range to understand the plasma wave environment in the inner magnetosphere, since several key wave modes that drive electron dynamics lie in the ELF/VLF range. In the presentation, we will show the average frequency spectra of electromagnetic fields in the measurement frequency range of OFA as a function of the L-shell and magnetic latitude for several magnetic local time sectors. Then the global distributions of the waves will be presented based on our statistical analysis. Considering these statistical investigations, we will discuss the excitation and propagation of ELF/VLF waves in the inner magnetosphere, along with their roles in its dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Relationship Between Pulsating Auroras and High-Latitude Chorus Wave Propagation Through Magnetospheric Density Ducts
presentations.abstract: Pulsating aurora, which is characterized by quasi-periodic luminosity modulation of ~2–20 sec, is a common aurora associated with ~10 keV electron precipitation. The precipitating electrons are scattered by whistler-mode chorus waves via wave-particle interactions. Recent studies have suggested that, during pulsating auroras, electrons with energies from tens to a few hundred of keV penetrate into lower altitudes and induce ozone depletion in the mesosphere and the upper stratosphere [Miyoshi et al., 2021; Oyama et al., 2017; Tesema et al., 2020]. In our previous study, we have observationally proposed a physical process in which wave propagation latitudes, the energy of scattered electrons, and patchy structures of pulsating auroras are controlled by “density ducts” in the magnetosphere [Ito et al., 2024]. However, the spatiotemporal distribution and generation processes of density ducts in the magnetosphere remain unclear. In this presentation, we specifically introduce the duct model proposed in our previous study, which explains the relationship between pulsating auroral morphology and high-latitude propagation of chorus waves. Based on this interpretation, we further report on a current analysis of pulsating auroras using ground-satellite conjugate observations from the perspective of density ducts and discuss the roles and formation of density ducts.

presentations.presentation_title: Dependence on the Velocity Distribution Functions of Energetic Electrons in the Generation Process of Whistler-mode Waves in the Magnetosphere
presentations.abstract: By performing a series of electron hybrid code simulations, we examine the effect of the initial velocity distribution function of energetic electrons on the generation of whistler-mode waves in the magnetosphere. Whistler-mode chorus emissions are coherent electromagnetic waves generated around the magnetic equator with frequency variation and play a crucial role in the evolution of radiation belt electrons. The generation process of chorus emissions has been explained by the nonlinear wave growth theory [Omura, EPS 2021] and reproduced in self-consistent numerical experiments [e.g., Katoh and Omura, GRL 2007; JGR 2011; JGR 2013; EPS 2016]. Previous studies revealed that the condition for chorus generation depends on the magnitude of the assumed temperature anisotropy in the electron velocity distribution function [Katoh et al., JGR 2018]. Recent studies suggest the importance of the kappa distribution in the generation process of whistler-mode waves [Summers and Stone, Phys. Plasmas 2025]. Simulation results demonstrate how the velocity distribution of energetic electrons influences the generation process of whistler-mode waves.

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Solar Active Regions: The Role of Magnetic Reconnection and Future Observational Perspectives
presentations.abstract: Active regions on the Sun originate from magnetic flux emerging from the deep convection zone. As these flux systems rise through the photosphere, chromosphere, and transition region into the corona, magnetic reconnection between field lines occurs, producing energetic phenomena such as Ellerman bombs and UV bursts. These small-scale events are believed to play a critical role in transporting magnetic energy upward and in shaping coronal structures, including loops and arcades. Despite their importance, simultaneous observations that cover the chromosphere, transition region, and corona have been scarce, leaving many questions about how magnetic energy release operates across these layers. The upcoming SOLAR-C mission, scheduled for launch in FY2028, aims to address this gap by providing unprecedented multi-layer observations with high spatial and temporal resolution. Equipped with advanced EUV spectrometer called the EUVST, SOLAR-C will enable detailed studies of dynamic processes in the atmospheres and their connections to coronal heating and solar eruptions. In this invited talk, we will review the significance of small-scale reconnection events, such as UV bursts, in the broader context of solar atmospheric dynamics. We will also introduce the SOLAR-C mission and its science objectives, highlighting how its capabilities will transform our understanding of magnetic energy transport from the lower atmosphere to the corona. The expected synergy between SOLAR-C, other missions, and state-of-the-art numerical simulations will also be discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Chromospheric Dynamics as a Key to Solar Atmospheric Coupling: Ground-based Observations at Hida Observatory
presentations.abstract: Recent advances in solar observations have significantly improved our understanding of the multi-layered solar atmosphere. In particular, ground-based observations have demonstrated their capability to capture chromospheric dynamics with high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution, providing essential diagnostics for energy and mass transport throughout the solar atmosphere. At Hida Observatory, Kyoto University, two solar telescopes are in operation: Domeless Solar Telescope (DST) and Solar Magnetic Activity Research Telescope (SMART). DST is a 60-cm vacuum telescope equipped with horizontal and vertical spectrographs, enabling high spatial resolution imaging and high-dispersion spectroscopy. Simultaneous multi-wavelength observations with DST enable detailed plasma diagnostics, such as the derivation of temperatures and non-thermal velocity distributions in prominences using appropriate line combinations. Spectro-polarimetric observations in the He I 1083 nm line have revealed magnetic field configurations that support quiescent filaments. In addition, high-cadence imaging observations of chromospheric fibrils in H-alpha +/- 0.05 nm obtained with the Universal Tunable Filter (UTF) have uncovered complex velocity structures in the lower solar atmosphere. SMART, particularly through the Solar Dynamics Doppler Imager (SDDI), provides Hα imaging spectroscopy at high temporal cadence. This capability enables systematic analyses of chromospheric velocity fields associated with flares, filament eruptions, and other dynamic phenomena. Using SDDI data, the three-dimensional kinematics of filament eruptions have been reconstructed with cloud-model techniques, and persistent transverse oscillations in prominences - likely associated with Alfvénic wave propagation - have been detected exclusively in Doppler velocity signals. Furthermore, ongoing studies aim to extend these solar investigations to stellar physics through Sun-as-a-star observational approaches. In this presentation, I will introduce recent scientific results obtained with DST and SMART, highlighting the role of chromospheric dynamics as a key element in coupling different layers of the solar atmosphere, and discuss future directions, including the development of the next-generation instrument, the Near-Infrared Tunable Filter (NIRTF).

presentations.presentation_title: Heating and Heat Conduction in the Transition Region of Coronal Loops
presentations.institution: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research
presentations.abstract: Traditional 1D coronal loop models suggest that the transition region is predominantly heated by heat conduction from the corona, at least if constant volumetric heating is assumed. However, when the spatial heating profile is modified, local energy deposition in the transition region can become more important. Recent advances in 3D MHD models enable the investigation of the relative roles of local heating and conductive energy gain in the transition region in a self-consistent way. For example, a recent study based on 3D MHD models suggests that plasma from the chromosphere to the corona in active region plages is heated through energy dissipation in local current sheets. However, this might not be the case in general. Using similar models, we find that the heat conduction might well dominate the heating of the transition region under certain conditions. Thus, the decade-old problem does not admit a simple yes-or-no answer, but requires detailed and quantitative analysis of the underlying heating mechanisms in different solar magnetic environments.

presentations.presentation_title: Three-dimensional and Multi-viewpoint Observations of Large-amplitude Prominence Oscillations
presentations.abstract: Large-amplitude oscillations of solar prominences/filaments provide a powerful tool for diagnosing magnetic structures, wave–prominence interactions, and eruption-related dynamics. However, single-viewpoint imaging often suffers from projection effects, making it difficult to distinguish longitudinal, transverse, vertical, horizontal, and rotational motions. In this presentation, I will summarize our recent studies of prominence oscillations based on multi-wavelength imaging, spectroscopy, and multi-viewpoint observations.These results demonstrate that three-dimensional and multi-viewpoint observations are essential for correctly interpreting prominence oscillations. They help reduce projection ambiguity, reveal mode coupling and energy conversion, and provide new diagnostics of magnetic configuration and pre-eruptive evolution in solar prominences.

presentations.presentation_title: Ultra-high-precision Measurements of Carbon-14 and Its Application for Space Weather Research
presentations.institution: Okinawa Institte of Science and Techonology
presentations.abstract: In this talk, we present recent progress in high-precision carbon-14 measurements in tree rings using Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS). Since the discovery of the extreme solar proton event in 774-775 CE, annual-resolution measurements of carbon-14 have been actively conducted worldwide. However, identification of sub-extreme solar proton events has still been challenging because of the difficulty in securing the stability of the measurement system. Therefore, the number of sub-extreme events identified remains limited. In this presentation, we demonstrate that detecting such sub-extreme events is possible with ultra-fine measurements of carbon-14 and that it is essential for accurately reconstructing both transient events and solar activity cycles. We also present that accurately distinguishing transient events and solar cycles enables us to discuss the solar cycle dependence of extreme events. Without achieving such precision, transient signals may be blended with solar-cycle signals. In this talk, we present a few examples of ultra-fine-precision measurements for the past millennium.

presentations.presentation_title: Ranking of the Extreme Forbush Decrease Events in 2024 and 2025 as Observed by Muon Detectors and Its Relationship with Solar Wind Parameters
presentations.abstract: Galactic cosmic ray intensity shows a transient variation known as Forbush decrease event, in association with the solar wind disturbances such as interplanetary shocks and coronal mass ejections. During the solar maximum of the solar cycle 25 in 2024 and 2025, we observed extremely large Forbush decreases by ground-based cosmic ray detectors. In particular, the June 2025 event was characterized by its extremely large amplitude and was accompanied by the high-speed solar wind of more than 1000 km/s. We show the historical ranking of this event using the long-term muon data observed with Nagoya muon detector in Japan, which has been continuously in operation since 1970. In addition, we investigate the relationship between the amplitude of large Forbush decrease events and solar wind parameters.

presentations.presentation_title: Stormtime Electric Fields at Middle and Low Latitudes as Observed by HF Doppler Sounders and Magnetometers During the Storm on May 10-11, 2024
presentations.institution: Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research, Nagoya University
presentations.abstract: During the storm on May 10-11, 2024, the geomagnetic sudden commencement (SC) was observed as SCx,y(PI,MI) (PI: preliminary impulse, MI: main impulse) in Bx,y-component. The SC at middle latitudes was SCx(+ - ) and SCy(- +) in the morning, and SCx(- +) and SCy(+ -) in the afternoon, and at the equator SCx(- +) on the day and SCx(+ -) in the night. During the storm main phase (MP), magnetic disturbances, MPx,y at middle latitudes was MPx(- ) and MPy(+) in the morning and MPx(+) and MPy(-) in the afternoon, and at the equator MPx(+) during the day and MP(-) in the night. The local time and latitude characteristics of PI and MI/MP are consistent with the DP2 currents driven by the dusk-to-dawn and dawn-to-dusk electric fields, respectively. The DP2 currents are composed of two-cell Hall current vortices at high-middle latitudes surrounding the foot of field-aligned currents and of Pedersen-Cowling currents between the foot of field-aligned currents and equatorial ionosphere. It is shown that the HF Doppler sounders in Japan observed eastward PI and westward MI/MP electric fields during the night, consistent with equatorial electrojet (EEJ) in the same meridian. It was found that the electric field and currents reversed their directions, i.e., overshielding occurred a few hours after the SC during the main phase, which caused rapid upward motion of the nighttime ionospheric F-layer over Japan. During the recovery phase of the storm on May 11 2024, several substorm positive bays occurred at mid-latitudes in the night, which were associated with DP2 currents on the dayside, same as the MI/MP currents. The HF Doppler sounders observed the dawn-to-dusk convection electric fields during the substorms, in contrast to the dusk-to-dawn overshielding electric fields that have often been observed during isolated substorms.

presentations.presentation_title: Advancing Solar Flare Forecasting: Operational Deployment of Physics-based Prediction NICT, Japan
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT), Japan
presentations.abstract: The National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) operates the only official space weather forecasting service in Japan. Reliable flare forecasting is critical for mitigating risks to satellites, communication systems, and power grids. Traditionally, NICT’s flare forecasts have relied on manual, empirical judgment, limiting the ability to issue timely alerts for severe events such as consecutive X-class flares in May 2024 and December 2025.To address this limitation, we have developed an automated warning system based on the physics-driven “κ-scheme” (Kusano et al., 2020), marking the first operational implementation of a physics-based flare prediction scheme in Japan. The system has been integrated into NICT’s forecasting workflow since October 2025 and successfully predicted several X-class flares, including those in late October and November 2025.In this study, we evaluate the flare prediction performance of the κ-scheme using X-class flares observed during Solar Cycle 25. In the presentation, we report the evaluation results and introduce NICT’s operational approach incorporating the κ-scheme.

presentations.presentation_title: Supersubstorm Auroral Current Systems Reproduced Using an Emulator with Superdarn Data Assimilation
presentations.institution: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology, Japan
presentations.abstract: Supersubstorms are extreme substorm events characterized by AE indices exceeding 2500 nT and are associated with strong auroral electrojet currents driven by intense solar wind driving. The associated ionospheric current systems differ substantially from those of isolated substorms, with isolated events dominated by nightside current enhancements, whereas supersubstorms exhibit pronounced local-time asymmetries characterized by significant auroral current intensification in the dawn and dusk sectors. In addition, shock-driven supersubstorms often produce highly localized current enhancements, especially on the dayside. Auroral current variations during isolated substorms on 30–31 October 2023 were reproduced (Nilam et al., in prep., 2026) using the SMRAI (Surrogate Model for the REPPU Auroral Ionosphere; Kataoka et al., 2024) emulator with SuperDARN data assimilation (SDDA; Nakano et al., 2025), demonstrating enhanced westward electrojets near midnight and realistic temporal fluctuations of auroral currents. The SMRAI emulator is trained on ionospheric outputs from the REPPU magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation, with the training dataset primarily covering around fifteen substorm events with AE in the range of 1500–2000 nT. As a result, direct application of the standard SDDA framework to supersubstorm conditions (AE > 2500 nT) represents a regime extrapolation and requires methodological modification. To address this issue, the SDDA framework was modified to prevent highly localized responses from being unrealistically mapped onto global current systems. With these modifications, the SSDA framework is able to reproduce both the standard auroral current systems associated with isolated substorms and the more complex, extreme currents during supersubstorms.

presentations.presentation_title: Spatiotemporal Evolution of the Earth's Ring Current During Extreme Geomagnetic Storms
presentations.abstract: Extreme geomagnetic storms provide a unique opportunity to examine the response of the ionosphere–magnetosphere system to extreme solar wind conditions. In this study, we investigate the spatiotemporal evolution of the ring current during extreme geomagnetic storms, with particular emphasis on identifying features that are unique to extreme events and those that can be understood as extensions of moderate storm-time processes. We analyze geomagnetic field data from a dense global network of low-latitude observatories (|MLAT| = 10–30°). Storm-time magnetic field perturbations are extracted by removing the quiet-time baseline and Sq variations, and UT–MLT maps are constructed using harmonic fitting techniques. The geomagnetic signatures are compared with upstream solar wind structures and, where available, in situ magnetospheric satellite observations to investigate the drivers of the observed ring current evolution. The geomagnetic field data reveal that extreme storms are characterized by intensified and long-lasting partial ring current signatures with pronounced magnetic local time (MLT) asymmetry. In contrast, moderate storms tend to exhibit strong MLT asymmetry primarily during the main phase, followed by a more symmetric configuration during the early recovery phase. While the overall intensification on the dusk side is common to both storm categories, extreme storms exhibit longer persistence of the dusk-side asymmetry, suggesting sustained open drift paths driven by extreme solar wind events. These findings imply that ring current dynamics during extreme storms involve strongly asymmetric pressure distributions in the inner magnetosphere, which can affect other key magnetospheric processes, such as radiation belt dynamics. Extreme events thus play an important role in clarifying how storm-time magnetospheric responses depend on the level of solar wind driving.

presentations.presentation_title: Earthquake Originated Pc3 Magnetic Pulsations and Their Generation Mechanism
presentations.abstract: The source of compressional Pc3 magnetic pulsations has been considered to be the plasma process in the solar wind or in the magnetosphere. However, the excitement of some of the Pc3s seems to be related to strong inland earthquakes that occur on the dayside. The Lamb waves generated by the Tonga undersea volcanic eruption in January 2022 are also believed to have excited large amplitude and short period compressional Pc3 geomagnetic pulsations in the dayside plasmasphere (Iyemori et al., 2025). A common epoch analysis shows an increase in power spectral density (PSD) in the Pc3 frequency band 10-30 minutes after the origin time of large inland earthquakes (M>6.5) during the daytime (10-14 LT). These observations suggest that the acoustic waves emitted by the ground motion at the earthquakes are the source of the Pc3s. In this presentation, we confirm the existence of the Pc3s excited by the earthquakes and discuss their generation mechanism.

presentations.presentation_title: Are Solar Flare-driven Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances Truly Sudden?
presentations.institution: Earthquake Research Institute, The University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: This study focuses on Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SID), a collective term for the rapid increase in ionization caused by enhanced X-ray and UV radiation. It is assumed that the SID occurs instantaneously and simultaneously on the entire dayside of the globe. In this work, we question this assumption by analysing 1-second resolution data of ionospheric total electron content (TEC) from worldwide distributed GNSS receivers. We study the global dayside TEC response to thirteen solar flares that occurred between 2003 and 2023, including eleven X-class and two M-class events. For the first time, high-temporal resolution allows to observe a high-speed apparent expansion of SID from the subsolar point toward the dawn/dusk region. We find that this expansion rate has a velocity from ~250-500 km/s, which may depend on the solar flare’s position on the solar disk. The expansion is due to the solar zenith angle impacting the magnitude of the ionospheric response and, consequently, causing the time delay between the TEC increase detected at the subsolar point and in dawn/dusk regions.This expansion is anisotropic i.e., depending on the observation’s location relative to the sub-solar point, and the velocity of the enhancement varies in a different part of the dayside of the ionosphere. This asymmetry can be explained by differences in the background conditions of the ionosphere and thermosphere at the time of the flare, which influence the amplitude of the TEC response and, therefore, the observed expansion velocity. We performed high-rate 10-second Thermosphere Ionosphere Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM) simulations that reproduced SID morphology and confirmed the flare enhancement expansion. Our work opens new horizons in the use of high-rate GNSS measurements for studies of the Earth’s ionosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Wind and Temperature Variability in the Upper Atmosphere Driven by Impulsive Sources
presentations.abstract: Large-scale changes in winds and temperatures in the upper atmosphere were seen frequently by the NASA ICON observatory to occur in response to impulsive inputs. The magnitude of the waves produced, and the depth in the thermosphere that their effects varies significantly and will be reviewed. Observations include examples of auroral forcing, and the more mysterious but clear effects of a migrating terminator wave. Only one natural hazard event from the lower atmosphere has been published using ICON observations to date: the Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai eruption. Here, we will present those results in brief, and we will present a survey of ICON observations from 2019–2022 during known natural hazard events.

presentations.presentation_title: Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances Observed During the 2024 Typhoon Shanshan: Effects of Atmospheric Waves and Electro-dynamical Forces
presentations.abstract: Here, we report findings on traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs) during typhoon Shanshan, using the total electron content (TEC) data derived from the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) network in Japan and Australia. TIDs with different propagating directions were observed during local nighttime over Japan. Southwestward and northeastward propagating TIDs exhibited clear conjugate signatures in the opposite hemisphere, whereas northwestward and southeastward propagating TIDs did not. We noticed the southwestward propagating TIDs were nearly in phase with their conjugate counterparts, while the northeastward propagating TIDs showed a distinct phase difference. The conjugate TIDs are thought to be primarily driven by polarization electric fields, which is related to the Pedersen conductivity variations, whereas the other TIDs represent passive ionospheric responses to typhoon‑induced gravity waves.

presentations.presentation_title: The Ionospheric Plasma Density Hole and Double-peak Structure During the May 2024 Mother's Day Storm
presentations.abstract: We employ in situ measurements from the advanced ionospheric probe (AIP) on FORMOSAT-5 (F5) and the ion velocity meter (IVM) on FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 (F7C2), alongside the global ionospheric specification (GIS) to investigate the ionospheric response to the great magnetic storm on 10 May 2024. These observations reveal a massive plasma density hole centered at the magnetic equator over the Atlantic sector during the midnight period. Within this depletion, F5/AIP at 720 km recorded upward ion velocities of about 245 m/s, whereas F7C2/IVM at 550 km simultaneously observed downward motions of approximately 106 m/s. GIS profiles further show a unique double-peak electron density structure with a lower peak at 440 km and an upper peak at 760 km altitude. These results indicate that the opposing vertical drifts at different altitudes are associated with the formation of the double-peak structure within the plasma hole.

presentations.presentation_title: Ionospheric Responses to the 12 November 2025 Geomagnetic Storm in Taiwan
presentations.abstract: This study investigates the dynamic response of the ionospheric F-region over Taiwan during the G4 geomagnetic storm of 12 November 2025. The event was triggered by an X5.1 flare from Region 4274 at 10:04 UTC on 11 November, with the associated coronal mass ejection (CME) reaching Earth at 00:00 UT on 12 November. The storm reached peak intensity with a planetary Kp index of 9- and a minimum Dst index of −238 nT at 05:00 UT. Locally, the Taiwan Disturbance Index (TWDI) registered a minimum of −326 nT at 11:26 UT. In this study, the high-resolution data from the ionosonde at Xinwu (25.0°N, 121.0°E) is used to examine the ionospheric responses. In addition, a network of 12 magnetometers is employed to derive the TWDI and characterize the storm-time Prompt Penetration Electric Fields (PPEF). Furthermore, radio-occultation (RO) and ion velocity meter (IVM) observations from the FORMOSAT-7/COSMIC-2 (F7/C2) provide critical vertical electron density profiles and in-situ ion drifts near Taiwan. This study provides the first multi-perspective evidence of a distinct vertical ionospheric stratification evolution over Taiwan during this extreme event.

presentations.presentation_title: A Simulation Study of Periodic Oscillations of the Upper Atmosphere Driven by Volcanic Eruptions
presentations.abstract: In intense volcanic eruptions, large-amplitude acoustic waves, Lamb waves, and gravity waves are generated through explosive expansion of the atmosphere. Those atmospheric waves propagate upward and cause significant disturbances in the thermosphere and ionosphere. One of the notable phenomena in the upper atmosphere associated with volcanic eruptions is periodic oscillations of the ionosphere with a period of about four minutes, which is likely to be driven by oscillations of the thermosphere. In the eruption of Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai on 15 January 2022, prominent periodic oscillations of the ionosphere were observed by various kinds of observations. Although previous studies suggest that the oscillations are associated with Lamb waves, the cause of the periodic oscillations in the upper atmosphere has not been fully understood. Recently a number of studies of the atmosphere and ionosphere have been done for the Tonga volcanic eruption. Although those studies elucidate the nature of Lamb waves, and gravity waves as well as traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs), the cause of the periodic oscillations have not been clearly explained. To investigate the periodic oscillations driven by volcanic eruptions, we have carried out the atmospheric simulations using a high-resolution two-dimensional nonhydrostatic atmosphere model. By applying a sudden local heat source to the model initially, acoustic waves, Lamb waves, and gravity waves as well as periodic oscillations are reproduced. The simulation results indicate that periodic oscillations in the atmosphere tend to develop after the passage of Lamb waves and that they are generated by the interaction between Lamb waves and thermospheric gravity waves. We will present the simulation results and discuss the cause of the oscillations by comparing with various observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Electron and Ion Acceleration in Reconnecting and Non-reconnecting Current Sheets in Shock-driven Turbulence
presentations.institution: University of Maryland, College Park; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center
presentations.abstract: In shock-driven turbulence, an abundance of current sheets can be produced by plasma instabilities, such as non-resonant ion-ion beam instability, and magnetic reconnection can occur in some of these current sheets. Electrons and ions can interact with both non-reconnecting and reconnecting current sheets in the shock-transition region and the downstream region. Performing two-dimensional fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, we investigate electrons’ and ions’ trajectories to elucidate energization mechanisms in those reconnecting and non-reconnecting current sheets in a quasi-parallel shock whose Alfvén Mach number exceeds 10. Electrons can be accelerated in magnetic islands proceed by ion-coupled reconnection, through the Hall electric field acceleration and the island betatron acceleration. Also, electrons can be accelerated in non-reconnecting current sheets that are thinning. Electrons energized by these mechanisms in the shock can form power-law energy spectra. Ions are also energized by those current sheets and magnetic islands. The ion temperature is significantly enhanced in magnetic islands because of the combination of the density reduction and the energization by the Hall electric field. In addition, when current sheets/magnetic islands are moving, ions can gain energy from the motional electric field, which works much more efficiently than the conventional shock-drift acceleration. We finally discuss that by multiple interactions with these current sheets both electrons and ions can reach the injection energy required by diffusive shock acceleration.

presentations.presentation_title: Cluster Observations of the Most Extreme Energetic Electron Acceleration Event in the Earth's Magnetotail
presentations.abstract: The energetic electrons in the Earth's magnetotail plays a crucial role in space weather. Although many studies have identified the basic processes of energetic electron acceleration, the conditions that lead to the most extreme acceleration events remain unclear. Here, we present a case study of one of the most extreme energetic electron acceleration events observed by the Cluster mission in the magnetotail over the entire lifetime of Cluster (2001-2024). The event occurred on October 3rd, 2007, at around 13:59, during a substorm when a corotating interaction region in the solar wind was crossing the Earth. The event is located in the transition region between the stretched tail and the dipole field and near the center of the current sheet. Our analysis reveals that multiple reconnection sites contribute differently to the event. The initial reconnection site creates a hot plasma sheet, and the subsequent acceleration on top of it, generated by subsequent reconnection sites, produces the high flux of energetic electrons. During the event, the magnetic flux tubes at spacecraft locations move back and forth. The peak total flux of energetic electrons is a superposition of two distinct populations energized by different adiabatic acceleration mechanisms: Fermi acceleration and betatron acceleration. Fermi acceleration occurs globally, while betatron acceleration is a local process. The comparison between auroral images and in-situ measurements shows that bursty bulk flows are in conjunction with the region showing auroral streamers evolving from poleward boundary intensifications.

presentations.presentation_title: Estimation of the reconnection rate from the SWCX emission at the dayside magnetopause
presentations.abstract: This invited talk will present numerical modeling of the Earth’s magnetosphere and its interaction with the solar wind, with a focus on the solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) process. We conducted high-resolution global MHD simulations of the magnetosphere and studied associated X-ray emissions via the SWCX process at the dayside magnetopause. Within the simulation data, virtual satellite observations revealed intensive X-ray emissions near the dayside magnetopause. Using high-resolution data and a synthesized X-ray map, we discern the topology of the dayside reconnection region, enabling us to estimate the reconnection rate geometrically. The implications of the present study for future missions, such as GEO-X and SMILE, will be discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Electron Crossover and Diffusion Region Width in Symmetric, Collisionless Magnetic Reconnection
presentations.abstract: We investigate electron-scale dynamics near the X-line during steady-state collisionless magnetic reconnection without a guide field, using fully kinetic Particle-In-Cell (PIC) simulations. By labeling electrons from opposite inflow regions, we examine the evolution of their bulk flows, force balance, and contributions to the electron current layer. The interpenetration of directed labeled flows from both sides gives rise to apparent off-diagonal pressure components, such that most of the contribution to the reconnection electric field arises from the crossover of electron flows originating from the two different inflow regions. We further show that the bulk acceleration of each electron population determines the size of the electron diffusion region (EDR) near the X-line. This work demonstrates how flow labeling provides new insights into reconnection structure, revealing behaviors that are otherwise inaccessible with conventional computational diagnostics.

presentations.presentation_title: Plasma Two-Fluid Simulation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
presentations.abstract: Low-temperature plasmas have a wide range of applications, including plasma processing, electric propulsion, and wall modeling in fusion devices. Among various plasma sources, helicon plasmas are particularly attractive due to their ability to generate high-density (~10¹⁹ m⁻³)with flexible device scalability. However, density limits have been observed in helicon discharges, and a detailed understanding of the underlying physical mechanisms is essential for their practical utilization. The density limit is thought to be associated with the coupled effects of neutral depletion in high-density regions and anomalous transport driven by drift-wave instabilities, mediated by transport and collisional effects. Capturing such coupled plasma–neutral dynamics requires a self-consistent treatment of sheath electric fields, which remains computationally demanding and challenges quantitative modeling of the density limit. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a mesh-free approach for solving partial differential equations by embedding governing equations directly into the loss function. This framework enables the enforcement of physical constraints without spatial discretization and offers flexibility and computational efficiency through automatic differentiation and GPU-based parallelization. Despite these advantages, applications of PINNs to plasma simulations that explicitly treat multiscale electron and ion fluid dynamics remain limited. In this study, we develop a foundational PINNs-based framework for two-fluid modeling of electrons and ions. The governing fluid equations, together with initial and boundary conditions, are embedded into the PINNs loss function and optimized to obtain the solution. To address the multiscale nature of the system, appropriate normalization is introduced, enabling robust and reliable predictions that agree well with conventional numerical methods. We further compare Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions and find that, while the Neumann condition achieves sufficient accuracy, the Dirichlet condition statistically enhances training stability. In addition, we discuss ongoing numerical investigations aimed at elucidating the physical mechanisms underlying the density limit.

presentations.presentation_title: Correlation Analysis Between Banded Chorus and Electron Density Enhancement Using Van Allen Probes Data
presentations.abstract: Banded chorus waves with a gap in intensity at half the equatorial electron cyclotron frequency (0.5 fce) is ubiquitous in the magnetosphere. One of the hypotheses for the gap formation involves localized density enhancements called density ducts. Therefore, a strong correlation between them in observational data can serve as strong evidence for that hypothesis. Here, we analyze the Van Allen Probes-A data to find density structures during banded chorus occurrences and investigate whether such correlations between them exist. Roughly 800 banded chorus events that accompany extended background density data (~2 hours) available were analyzed in detail. It is shown that only 28% of the banded chorus events are found to occur with localized enhancements whose peak-to-base density ratio is greater than 1.3, whereas roughly 50% are associated with smaller-magnitude density irregularities. For the 28% events, the typical radial extent of the ducts is 10~600 km and the peak-to-base density ratio is < ~3. However, it does not appear that the lower band waves and density duct parameters is strong enough to warrant the said hypothesis as being the primary mechanism for the power gap formation.

presentations.presentation_title: Cascade and Damping of Compressible Turbulence: Theory Vs. Observations
presentations.abstract: Compressible turbulence plays a central role in mediating energy transfer across scales in space and astrophysical plasmas. In this work, we present recent advances in both theoretical and observational studies of compressible turbulence. Using large-scale kinetic simulations, we investigate turbulence–particle interactions and demonstrate that damping at magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) scales quantitatively agrees with transit-time damping theory, even within fully developed nonlinear states. Remarkably, the turbulent cascade persists despite intermittent phase steepening, revealing the robustness of cross-scale energy transfer. Furthermore, by applying an improved compressible MHD mode decomposition algorithm to Cluster spacecraft observations, we show that magnetic anisotropy in solar wind turbulence is strongly mode-dependent. Specifically, Alfvénic fluctuations exhibit a broad distribution of propagation angles. In contrast, compressible modes are predominantly concentrated near the quasi-parallel (slab-like) direction—consistent with our theoretical and numerical results on damping. Together, these results bridge kinetic simulations and in situ measurements, advancing our understanding of compressible turbulence.

presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Variation of the Mean Wind Field in the Antarctic Lower Thermosphere
presentations.abstract: The middle frequency (MF) radar at Syowa station, Antarctica (69S, 39E), has continuously been observing horizontal winds in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere since 1999. In addition to the conventional correlation analysis wind measuring technique [Briggs, 1984], a meteor wind technique has also been adopted for the Syowa system [Tsutsumi and Aso, 2005]. Because of its low radio frequency (2.4 MHz) the MF meteor winds can be estimated up to 120 km in contrast to the conventional VHF (~30 MHz) meteor radars, where the upper limit is around 105 km. The MF meteor wind technique has recently been updated, and all the existing raw data since 1999 has been reprocessed, now providing much finer time/spatial resolution wind information than before. In this study we examine the long-term variation of the Antarctic mesosphere and lower thermosphere winds based on the quarter century of wind data, with an emphasis on the lower thermosphere, where a long-term wind trend has rarely been estimated because of the lack of observation techniques in the region.. presentations.presentation_title: Himawari/ahi Observations of Polar Mesospheric Cloud Variations Associated with the 2022 Tonga Eruption
presentations.abstract: Polar mesospheric clouds (PMCs) are water ice clouds, which are considered to be highly sensitive to temperature and water vapor. The potential relationship between large volcanic eruptions and PMC activities has been discussed since the 1883 Krakatoa eruption. However, this relationship remains poorly understood due to a lack of effective observational data and the rarity of such large-scale events. The Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai (HTHH) submarine volcanic eruption on 15 January 2022 was a large-scale event that injected an unprecedented amount of water vapor into the stratosphere. This injected water vapor subsequently spread globally, reaching the polar mesopause regions approximately two years after the eruption. Thus, the 2022 HTHH event would be a nice opportunity to examine the relationship between large volcanic eruptions and PMC activities. To investigate this event, we analyzed the PMC occurrence rate (OR) data from the Himawari-8/AHI and Himawari-9/AHI, as well as temperature and water vapor volume mixing ratio (H 2 O VMR) data from the Aura/Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS). In our analysis, we focused on the eruption-injected water vapor effects on the PMC OR variations. To extract the effects of water vapor on the PMC variations, we reproduced the temperature-dependent PMC OR variability components. Then, we remove the reproduced components and derive residuals as temperature-independent components in the PMC OR variability, denoted as ∆PMC. As a result, we found a significant ∆PMC increase (+13.3–17.1%) in January 2024, i.e., two years after the 2022 HTHH eruption, in the Southern Hemisphere (SH). The obtained ∆PMC increase was associated with a significant increase in H 2 O VMR (+0.87±0.04 ppmv compared to 2016–2021 mean). These results would indicate a relationship between the large volcanic eruptions and PMC activities based on the observations.

presentations.presentation_title: Deep Learning Enabled Determination of Direction of Propagation of Ripples in Images of OH Airglow Observed over Gurushikhar Using a Very High Temporal and Spatial Resolution Shortwave Infrared Imager (SIRI)
presentations.institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Kalyani
presentations.abstract: Dynamical and convective instabilities generate ripples when gravity waves (GW) break in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT) region. Ripples look similar to GW in airglow images but are much smaller with a lifetime of up to 45 minutes and spatial horizontal scales of 5-15 km and thus can be observed only in high resolution (spatial and temporal) airglow observations. Their detection as well as understanding their properties will throw light on their generation mechanism and dynamics of the region. In the current study, ripples in OH airglow images obtained over Gurushikhar (24.7°N 72.8°E), Mt. Abu in Rajasthan, India, using Shortwave InfraRed Imager (SIRI) are investigated. Data was recorded every 20 secs from 19:00 hr to 07:00 hr next day from 22-31 January 2024 and corresponding images are obtained through image differencing method. You Look Only Once (YOLO) version-11 with pre-trained weights as part of transfer learning is used as an object detection method to obtain the bounding box coordinates of the detected ripples in airglow images. A few prior works that used deep learning in GW studies emphasized the classification task in airglow images and very few focused on detection of the GW in the image. As YOLO is a single stage detector, it performs well with a balanced computational speed. Ripples in airglow images are obtained with good precision (mean average precision of 0.62). Non-max suppression is applied for multiple and overlapping bounding boxes. Coordinates of correct predicted boxes over ripples are then considered to extract the direction of propagation and the results are validated through manual checking. The results show that the ripples are initially predominant in the Southwest direction over Gurushikhar, then change direction to Southeast around midnight followed by changing to Northeast and finally Northwest by dawn.

presentations.presentation_title: Medium-scale Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances Driven by Secondary Gravity Waves Associated with Record-breaking Heavy Rainfall in August 2021 Over Kyushu, Japan.
presentations.abstract: Beginning on 11 August August, 2021, moist air flowed into Kyushu (southwestern Japan), intensifying a stationary front and leading to record-breaking precipitation. At around 17 UT on 12 August, the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) captured concentric stratospheric gravity waves (GWs) over the heavy rainfall region. ~6 hours later, Japan and Korea’s GNSS networks detected medium-scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (MSTIDs) originating near Fukuoka, Kyushu (~131 E, ~32.5 N) and propagating from northward to southward directions. Our backward ray-tracing analysis using SD-WACCM-X suggests that the concentric GWs converged around (~133 E, ~32.5 N, ~70–100 km altitude) at ~22 UT and were unlikely to have propagated upward from below the stratosphere. Meanwhile, as for the stratospheric GWs, our forward ray-tracing analysis using JAWARA suggests that the observed stratospheric GWs broke up in the mesosphere at ~18–20 UT, producing an eastward local body force around the convergence area of the GWs driving the MSTIDs. This breaking, however, occurred 2–4 hours earlier than the potential generation time (~22 UT). To explore the source of the stratospheric GWs, we performed a convection-resolving meteorological simulation below ~48 km altitude using the WRF model. The simulation successfully reproduced stratospheric GWs similar to those observed by AIRS, continuously emitted from deep convection within the heavy rainfall between 17 and 24 UT. This continuous GW emission can explain the time gap between the primary GW breaking and secondary GW generation. We conclude that the MSTIDs were driven by the secondary GWs, which were generated by the breaking of convectively-generated primary GWs.This research was supported by Global–Learning & Academic research institution for Master's PhD students, and Postdocs (LAMP) Program of the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Ministry of Education (no. RS-2024-00442483).

presentations.presentation_title: Observations and Modeling of the Migrating Four-Hour Tide in the Middle Atmosphere
presentations.abstract: The characteristics of the hexadiurnal, or four-hour, tide are analyzed by observation and modeling. According to satellite observations of horizontal winds, the four-hour oscillation shows a horizontal structure with a zonal wavenumber of six, which corresponds to the migrating hexadiurnal tide (HW6). This signal is observed across a wide altitude range in the lower to middle thermosphere. The HW6 tide is also found to occur in whole-atmosphere model simulations. Additionally, the meridional structure and seasonal variation are examined. Around the solstices, the HW6 amplitude is enhanced in the winter hemisphere. Another amplitude peak is observed about one month before and after the equinox, but not during the equinox. The latter is explained by the seasonal progression of the dominant Hough mode in the heating rate in the stratopause. However, the former is not explained by this mechanism, since the dominant Hough mode in the temperature response differs from that in the heating. The excitation of the secondary mode is explained by mode coupling, using modified linear shallow water equations. The results indicate the important role of advection due to the background zonal wind, rather than the meridional gradient of the zonal wind. The zonal advection term is interpreted as a combination of a mode and the background wind, which is anti-symmetric with respect to the equator, producing a mode one order higher. This mechanism is only important around the solstices, because the background wind is nearly symmetric around the equinoxes.

presentations.presentation_title: Large-scale Gravity Waves in the Thermosphere and Their Impacts Using Icon-mighti and Sd-waccmx
presentations.abstract: Large-scale gravity waves (GWs) with zonal wavelength of 800-5000 km are extracted and analyzed from the Specified Dynamics version of WACCMX (SD-WACCMX) outputs from January 2020 to January 2021. First, large-scale GWs from SD-WACCMX are validated against GW observations from Michelson Interferometer for Global High-resolution Thermospheric Imaging (MIGHTI) instruments on the Ionospheric Connection Explorer (ICON). Both MIGHTI and SD-WACCMX show similar seasonal variations in the latitude range of 0°-40°N with clear semi-annual variations with peaks in December-January and July-August below 200 km. After the validation with MIGHTI observations, SD-WACCMX GWs are used to calculate GW drag to study GW impacts on background wind structures. Average resolved large-scale GW drag is ~15 ms -1 day -1 , which is about 20-30% of parameterized GWs in SD-WACCMX. For short-term variations, resolved large-scale GW drag can exceed ~40 ms -1 day -1 during the 2021 stratospheric sudden warming (SSW). Sensitivity studies using SD-WACCMX to identify sources of GWs will be presented.
