presentations.presentation_title: Temporal and Spatial Evolution of Fine Structures of the Es Layer by Using Ultra-dense GNSS Network Data
presentations.institution: National Institute of Maritime, Port and Aviation Technology
presentations.abstract: The Sporadic E (Es) layer is an ionospheric layer which has very high density but is thin in altitude occurring in the E region. The electron density of the Es layer is so high that radio waves even at VHF band can be reflected and propagate beyond horizon to cause interference. It has been well known that the Es layer is formed by the vertical shear of the neutral wind. However, the occurrence of the Es layer is still difficult to predict due to its "sporadic" nature. We used ROTI (rate of TEC (total electron content) index) derived from ultra-dense GNSS network over Japan and showed one case where the Es layer was generated, propagated, changed its complex form at scale sizes of about 10km (Saito et al., 2025). To further improve the temporal and spatial resolution, we used ROTI values derived from high sampling rate data with a short average interval. Results of analysis of multiple Es events with the method will be reported at the conference. The SoftBank’s GNSS observation data used in this study was provided by SoftBank Corp. and ALES Corp. through the framework of the ”Consortium to utilize the SoftBank original reference sites for Earth and Space Science”.

presentations.presentation_title: High-frequency Gravity Wave Characteristics Revealed by the Condor Multi-static Radar in the Andes
presentations.abstract: CONDOR is a multi-static meteor radar network that measures neutral wind in the mesopause region (80-110 km) over the Andes (30.3S, 70.7W). Due to its high meteor detection rate (reach about 100,000 per day), reliable measurement of horizontal and vertical wind profiles in the mesopause region can be achieved at very high temporal resolutions (5 min), which enable identification and characterization of high frequency gravity waves (with periods as short as 30 min) continuously throughout its multi-year observations. In this presentation, both individual case studies and multi-year statistics of high frequency gravity waves will be presented. The analysis reveals a large variety of gravity waves, with both upward and download propagations, and seasonal varying horizontal propagation directions. These characteristics are linked to the varying background wind and influence of atmospheric tides and planetary waves.

presentations.presentation_title: Lower Atmospheric Forcing of the ITM System: DYNAMIC Observations of Zonal Wind Responses to Stratospheric Variability
presentations.institution: The Catholic University of America/ NASA GSFC
presentations.abstract: Sudden Stratospheric Warmings (SSWs), characterized by dramatic stratospheric temperature increases, profoundly influence high-latitude thermospheric zonal winds, presenting significant space weather challenges. A critical gap persists in understanding these dynamics, particularly during quiet winter conditions, necessitating the isolation of SSW-induced responses from seasonal variability to reveal the phenomenon's intrinsic behavior under solar and geomagnetically quiet conditions. This study explores the ways in which data from the DYNAMIC mission will be useful in addressing this gap.We analyze synthetic DYNAMIC data sampled from the SD-WACCM-X model, in a notional measurement configuration consistent with the science target outlined in the Decadal Survey (two-point altitude profiles of winds/temperatures from 90-300 km altitude). This DYNAMIC-modeled synthetic dataset serves as the core for our analysis, which includes characterization of thermospheric zonal wind variability and SSW events.Our results reveal SSW-induced thermospheric responses, showcasing significant zonal wind variability directly linked to the stratospheric temperature rising due to the SSWs. This work provides compelling evidence that a notional DYNAMIC configuration consistent with the Decadal Survey science target will be able to detect and delineate the substantial role of lower atmosphere dynamics in influencing thermospheric wind changes. This highlights DYNAMIC's critical importance for advancing our understanding of ionosphere-thermosphere coupling, ultimately enhancing space weather predictability and operational resilience.

presentations.presentation_title: Chromospheric Dynamics of an Umbral Flare Kernel Based on Coordinated SUNRISE-III/SCIP and Hida/DST Observations
presentations.abstract: We present coordinated ground-based spectroscopic observations of an M1.4 solar flare that occurred in the NOAA Active Region 13738 on 2024 July 13, focusing on the chromospheric dynamics of compact flare kernels formed within a sunspot umbra. The observations were obtained through a joint campaign between the infrared spectropolarimetric instrument SCIP onboard SUNRISE-III and Domeless Solar Telescope (DST) at Hida Observatory, Kyoto University. Simultaneous imaging spectroscopy in multiple chromospheric lines, including Ca II 8498/8542, K I D2, H-alpha, and Na I D1/D2, enables us to investigate the temporal evolution and spectral characteristics of flare kernels in the umbra at high spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution. While significant intensity enhancements are detected in these chromospheric diagnostics, no corresponding brightening is observed in photospheric lines. High-resolution SCIP observations resolve fine-scale substructures within the flare kernel at approximately 1000 km. The spectral profiles show spatial and temporal variations in Doppler shifts and line widths, characterizing the dynamic behavior of chromospheric plasma in sunspot umbrae during the flare. These observations provide information on chromospheric plasma responses to energy input from the corona associated with the flare.

presentations.presentation_title: Stereoscopic Diagnostics of the Solar Convection: Two Components of the Velocity Field Vector Using Solar Orbiter and Hinode
presentations.abstract: Convection at the solar surface provides the energy source for atmospheric heating and drives various magnetic activities. To link these energy transfer processes, one of the key issues lies in deriving the velocity and magnetic field vectors, particularly their horizontal components, because gas flows at the solar surface can interact with vertically-oriented magnetic flux tubes that extend into the upper atmosphere. A promising approach is to use stereoscopic observations, incorporating multiple LOS components obtained from different viewing angles. The joint use of the Solar Orbiter / Polarimetric Helioseismic Imager (SO/PHI) and Hinode / Spectropolari-meter (SP) is well-suited for studying small-scale features, thanks to their stable space-based observations and comparable high spatial resolution.We analyzed a quiet region, observed at cosine of heliocentric angles of 0.80 (Hinode) and 0.90 (Solar Orbiter), with a 63-degree separation angle between the Sun-Hinode and Sun-SO lines. Our newly developed coalignment algorithm, applicable to slit-based and filtergraph observations, generates a map that is coaligned in both space and time, with the same number of spatial pixels and a correlation coefficient of 0.91, enabling one-to-one pixel comparison. The velocity field vector is derived by decomposing the two LOS velocities into the vertical and horizontal flow components, based on their respective heliocentric angles. The resulting horizontal flow field reveals clear signatures of fountain-like divergent flow in granules. This behavior is naturally expected from convection theory, but it is the first observational validation using Doppler measurements. In addition, our method captures horizontal flows along intergranular lanes, which may contribute to shaping meso-scale distribution of magnetic fluxtubes beyond the granulation scale. This presentation explores the horizontal flow distribution, and discusses the potential of stereoscopic diagnostics for quiet regions.

presentations.presentation_title: Full-disk Analysis On The Wave Propagation From The Solar Photosphere To The Chromosphere
presentations.abstract: It is important to clarify the relationship between waves and magnetic fields in order to understand chromospheric and coronal heating. In this study, we analyzed time-series data spanning more than 12 hours of chromospheric velocity fields in the Hα line obtained with SMART/SDDI at Hida Observatory of Kyoto University, as well as photospheric velocity fields from SDO/HMI, and examined the spatial distributions of oscillation power and phase differences over the entire solar disk. Furthermore, restricting to quiet-Sun regions, we investigated the center-to-limb variations of the power and phase differences. As a result, in addition to the 3-minute and 5-minute oscillations commonly observed in the chromosphere, we found that long-period oscillations on the order of 20 minutes are present throughout the solar disk in the chromosphere. These long-period oscillations show a strong spatial correlation with magnetic regions, including the chromospheric network regions in quiet-Sun, and also exhibit larger power toward the limb. Such long-period oscillations have rarely been reported in previous studies due to the limited duration of observations. Next, for the 3-minute and 5-minute oscillations, we found that the power in the Hα line-core velocities decreases toward the limb. We also found that oscillation amplitudes at both periods have a hump at heliocentric angle of 50 degree. If we interprete these oscillations as slow-mode waves, this implies that they propagate efficiently in the chromosphere where the magnetic field lines are inclined by about 50 degrees from the vertical. In this presentation, we will introduce these results and discuss them with a focus on the relationship between power and phase differences and magnetic field structures.

presentations.presentation_title: Magnetic Connectivity of Multiple Bipolar Pairs Below the Photosphere in the Super Active Region AR3664 in May 2024
presentations.abstract: In May 2024, the super active region AR3664 erupted with a series of intense solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), triggering significant interplanetary and geoeffective impacts. Within this active region, multiple bipolar pairs emerged successively and underwent strong interactions. For such a complex magnetic configuration of the active region, what does the corresponding magnetic structure below the photosphere look like? Based on the observations from Spaceweather HMI Active Region Patch (SHARP), we perform magnetic field reconstruction and flux evolution analysis. The results indicate that these bipolar pairs belong to the same magnetic topological system below the photosphere, manifesting as interconnected multi-arch structures. Driven by convection and magnetic buoyancy, the arch structures at different depths gradually rise to the photosphere, forming the observed bipolar pairs. Our work reveals the magnetic connectivity of complex bipolar pairs beneath the photosphere, providing a new perspective on the association and emergence process of multiple bipolar pairs. This study contributes to the understanding of the magnetic field distribution and evolution in super active regions from a holistic perspective.

presentations.presentation_title: 3D magnetic structures triggering an M-class flare observed with SUNRISE III/SCIP
presentations.abstract: The international balloon-borne observatory SUNRISE III successfully conducted high-resolution, high-precision polarization observations with no atmospheric turbulence during its flight in July 2024. SUNRISE III observed an M5.4-class flare on July 13 th . The 3-hour observation began at 11:44 UT, one hour before the GOES X-ray flux peaked at 12:40 UT. SCIP obtained full Stokes profiles in the 770 nm and 850 nm range, covering the photospheric Fe I 849 nm, the upper photospheric K I 766 nm and 770 nm, and the chromospheric Ca II 849 nm and 854 nm lines. The FOV of SCIP covered a part of the polarity inversion line (PIL) in the active region, where complex Stokes V profiles appeared in the photospheric lines. The Stokes inversion found that these profiles can be explained by a two-component atmosphere with both magnetic polarities. The non-linear force-free-field extrapolation suggests that the magnetic fields have a bold patch structure on the PIL. We will discuss the relation between these magnetic field structures and the flare activity.

presentations.presentation_title: Magnetic Field Diagnostics of a Solar Active Region Filament
presentations.institution: Institute of Space and Astronautical Science, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency
presentations.abstract: Solar filaments are dense and cool plasma structures suspended in the solar corona by magnetic fields. To better understand the magnetic environments of active-region (AR) filaments and the formation of spectral line polarization, we performed the He I 10830 angstrom spectropolarimetric observations of an AR filament. In the observed filament, we found some pixels which show Zeeman-like profiles showing double-peaked symmetric profiles in optically thick regions (τ>1). Full-Stokes inversions with the HAZEL code were carried out with two cases; one takes into account the Zeeman and the Hanle effects, the other takes into account only the Zeeman effect. For the former and the latter cases, we name the full and the reduced atomic polarization inversions, respectively. The reduced atomic polarization inversion returned an unrealistically strong magnetic field (~500 G), which is difficult to reconcile with standard magnetic field models in which the field strength decreases with height from the photosphere to the chromosphere, given that simultaneous Si I 10827 angstrom observations indicate photospheric magnetic field of less than 100 G. We therefore adopted the full atomic polarization solution, which yielded a mean field strength of 101 ± 33 G and a horizontal field nearly parallel to the filament axis, making the distinction between two classical normal and reverse polarity models has no physical significance. The Zeeman-like profiles are interpreted as the combined result of multiple-scattering depolarization and partial frequency redistribution (PRD) effects. Our results highlight the need to incorporate PRD physics in modeling He I 10830 angstrom polarization in optically thick objects.

presentations.presentation_title: Penetrating Waves Along Spicules to the Corona
presentations.institution: The Graduate University for Advanced Studies, SOKENDAI
presentations.abstract: Alfvénic waves, observed as the transverse motion of spicules (jets extending along magnetic field lines) in the chromosphere, are among the most promising candidates for heating the solar corona and accelerating the solar wind in polar coronal holes. Here, we investigated a statistical study of Alfvénic waves propagating along spicules in polar coronal holes using the Si IV spectra observed by the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph (IRIS) to determine whether sufficient wave energy is carried to the corona, even considering wave reflection at the transition region. We developed a technique for wave detection, wave-mode identification, and energy flux estimation for each detected wave by the line-of-sight (LOS) velocity and intensity. Alfvénic waves were detected, consisting of 46 ascending Alfvénic waves and 28 descending Alfvénic waves. Considering the random transverse oscillation toward the LOS direction and some fraction of ascending waves are reflected at the transition region and observed as descending waves, the energy flux of the waves penetrating to the corona is 1.2x10 5 erg cm -2 s-1 . We also found multiple velocity components in the observed spectra, which indicate that the energy flux should be underestimated by 4-9 times smaller. We estimated the penetrating energy flux to the corona for the first time and showed that Alfvénic waves transport enough energy for the coronal heating and the solar wind acceleration, even considering the wave reflection at thetransition region.

presentations.presentation_title: Formation Mechanism of Short-period Quasi-periodic Pulsations in Radio Bursts
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: We will present imaging analyze results of radio quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) which occurred on 11 th November 2014 observed by MingantU SpEctral Radioheliograph (MUSER). Although the phenomenon of radio QPPs has been known for over fifty years, high frequency, temporal and spatial resolution's spectral imaging of sub-second QPPs in the radio waveband remains scarce. MUSER recorded a total of four groups of QPPs, occurring between 05:05 and 06:35 UT during a no CME and before a C-class flare period. All QPPs exhibited the similar sub-second periods with frequencies ranging from 1.0 to 2.0 GHz and no significant group frequency drift. Radio imaging was achieved by combining 399 selected baselines. The radio sources are occurrence right around AR 12205 after imaging and comparing with AIA/SDO images. The AIA/SDO in EUV, GOES in soft X-ray and Fermi in 6-25 KeV also observed the relevant emissions enhancement although there is no dramatic flare activity. These findings suggest that the observed QPPs were independent of any major flare or CME, but may have the relationship with the pre-flare activity. We shall investigate the dynamic spectrum evolution characteristics of the radio QPPs, as well as the spatial evolution of the radio sources in different frequencies and groups. We will also discuss here the possible formation mechanism of the plasma about the sub-second QPPs before they propagate in the upper atmosphere which shall help us contribute to a deeper understanding of the nature of QPPs in solar radio emissions.

presentations.presentation_title: Development of a Next-Generation Interplanetary Scintillation Observation System for Space Weather Forecasting
presentations.abstract: Interplanetary scintillation (IPS) is a powerful remote-sensing technique for monitoring solar wind speed and density across interplanetary space. At the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE), Nagoya University, IPS observations have been conducted for over 50 years using dedicated radio telescopes in Japan. Our current 327 MHz IPS system reconstructs global solar wind structures in the inner heliosphere and detects transient events such as coronal mass ejections (CMEs) far from the Sun, contributing to space weather research and forecasting. To further enhance these capabilities, we are developing a next-generation IPS system based on two-dimensional phased-array antennas. The planned array consists of five offset cylindrical parabola antennas aligned east–west, each with a north-south axis, a diameter of 8 m, and a length of 100 m, providing a total collecting area of about 4,000 m 2 . Along the focal line of each cylinder, 1,024 high-sensitivity dipole antennas are densely deployed, enabling wide-field observations covering 120° north-south and 7° east-west. Signals from all dipoles are fully digitized and processed using FPGA-based digital signal processing, enabling simultaneous multi-beam formation and concurrent observations of many radio sources. A prototype array corresponding to about 30% of the full system is currently under development at the Fuji Observatory. To improve the physical interpretation of IPS data, we utilize global magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations. Synthetic IPS signals are computed by solving radio wave scattering equations along each line of sight using simulated heliospheric plasma distributions, enabling direct comparisons with observations and improving the reliability of MHD-based space weather forecasts. Achieving accurate real-time space weather forecasting requires an operational framework in which IPS observations and IPS-assimilated global MHD simulations can be executed promptly.

presentations.presentation_title: Review of the New Fitting Model for IPS Single-station Observation
presentations.abstract: Radio waves from compact sources, such as quasars, are scattered by electron density fluctuations in the solar wind. This phenomenon is known as interplanetary scintillation (IPS). Ground-based IPS observation is an effective method for remote sensing of the solar wind, and the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) has been conducting multi-station IPS observations for over 50 years. Single-station analysis has been explored to derive solar wind velocity through model fitting of power spectra, which would enable data acquisition even when multi-station observations are unavailable. However, in many cases, parameter degeneracy prevented the accurate estimation of solar wind velocity.The purpose of this study is to solve this issue. While a general approach to resolve this degeneracy is to constrain parameters other than the target, parameters such as the spectral index alpha and source size theta vary with each observation in IPS analysis.Therefore we devised a new fitting method for single-station analysis using a simple model function that captures the structural features of the IPS power spectrum. To validate this new method, we compared the derived velocities with In-situ observations from the OMNI dataset, following the approach of Coles et al.(1978). The results demonstrate that the derived solar wind velocity achieves analytical accuracy comparable to the obtained velocity from the ISEE multi-station analysis. This study enables the extraction of more detailed solar wind information from IPS observations. Combined with IPS-tomography analysis, this method will contribute to understanding of the solar wind structure. In this presentation, we will introduce the details of this newly devised method.

presentations.presentation_title: Magnetic Field Fluctuations and Passage of a CME in the Middle Corona Investigated by Faraday Rotation Technique Using Akatsuki Spacecraft Radio Waves
presentations.abstract: Understanding behaviors of magnetic fields and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) waves in the middle solar corona (1.5–6.0 R S ) is essential for clarifying the energy transport processes that contribute to coronal heating and solar wind acceleration. Faraday rotation (FR) measurements are among the most effective tools for investigating magnetic fields in these regions. In this study, we retrieved the FR time series from the X-band signals transmitted by the Akatsuki spacecraft to obtain magnetic field profiles in the middle corona. By comparing the FR data with the electron column density obtained simultaneously, we identified that the FR fluctuations at 1.7 R S as magnetic field oscillations related to Alfvén waves. We also detected FR fluctuations with a large amplitude, representing a passage of a coronal mass ejection (CME) event at 2.5 R S . Furthermore, the standard deviation of the magnetic field was derived using an empirical model of the background electron density and an empirical model of magnetic field. According to these estimations, we suggested that at most ~0.02–1.5% of energy flux of Alfvén waves may be converted to that of slow magnetosonic waves. These findings contribute to improve understanding of MHD wave behavior and CME evolution in the middle corona. In this presentation, we will highlight the key results of our recent paper (under review) and updates related to the Faraday rotation measurements.

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-point Validation of Global Solar Wind Simulation at L1 and Parker Solar Probe Using Different Synoptic Maps
presentations.abstract: The reproducibility of heliospheric structures in numerical models depends on the choice of the input photospheric magnetic field synoptic map. The global three-dimensional (3D) magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation code, SUSANOO, utilizes the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) mrbqs synoptic map series (hereafter GONGb) with a daily cadence. Previous comparative studies utilizing coronal structure simulation such as potential-field source-surface (PFSS) models reported discrepancies between coronal structures derived from GONGb and in-situ observations. These inconsistencies likely originate from instrumental zero-point offsets present in the raw magnetograms. Unlike the zero-point corrected mrzqs series (hereafter GONGz), the GONGb dataset retains these observational artifacts, which subsequently propagate into the PFSS extrapolation and the heliospheric model. This study examines solar wind simulations modeled by SUSANOO using four distinct synoptic maps: the GONGb, the GONGz, the ADAPT-GONG map (hereafter ADAPTg) incorporating data assimilation, and the space-based SDO/HMI map. We compare the simulation results with in-situ measurements using root mean square error and correlation coefficient from OMNI (L1) and the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) during the solar minimum period from 2019/01/01, to 2019/12/31. The simulation driven by GONGb exhibited the lowest values at both L1 and PSP locations among all input maps, which is consistent with previous reports. In contrast, GONGz, ADAPTg, and HMI yielded comparable performance on L1. The performance of GONGz was marginally superior to other models with respect to the magnetic field measured by PSP, corroborating prior research. These results suggest the importance of zero-point correction in solar wind modeling. Overall, the GONGz map yielded the most consistent agreement with in-situ measurements in the SUSANOO simulation. This study provides a validation framework for global MHD models that are widely used in radio diagnostics such as interplanetary scintillation (IPS).

presentations.presentation_title: Event and Statistical Evidence for Ulf-controlled Ducting of Whistler-mode Waves
presentations.institution: 1. Tohoku University, 2. Institute of Atmospheric Physics, Czech Academy of Science, 3. Charles University
presentations.abstract: Whistler-mode waves are a key driver of the radiation belt through efficient wave-particle interaction. Because cyclotron resonance energy increases away from the near-equatorial source region, clarifying the conditions that enable high-latitude propagation is crucial for the radiation-belt dynamics. In this study, we provide evidence of ultralow-frequency (ULF)-controlled ducting propagation of whistler-mode waves via event analysis and statistical survey to demonstrate when and where ULF waves create conditions favorable for duct-like guiding of whistler-mode waves. First, we analyze a representative Cluster event on 19 February 2019, in which whistler-mode chorus wave intensity observed at a magnetic latitude around 19° exhibits clear modulation synchronized with the ULF oscillation. The chorus wave corresponds to the increase in refractive index caused by the ULF wave. The wave vector direction presents the consistency of ducted propagation. Second, we perform a statistical analysis using 12 years of Cluster C1/C2 observations from 2010 to 2021 and 8 years of Arase observations from 2017 to 2024. We identify 375 candidate ducting/modulation events by requiring (i) whistler-mode wave intensity modulation with a period comparable to the accompanying ULF oscillation or (ii) enhancement occurring at a specific phase of the compressional ULF component, evaluated at magnetic latitude ≥ 10° to emphasize propagation effects. Occurrence mapping shows that the peak occurrence rate reaches 10% at MLT = 6–9 with high solar wind velocity (>600km/s) or high dynamic pressure (4 nPa). Events preferentially occur under toroidal-dominant ULF. This suggests that externally driven ULF waves, which efficiently excite toroidal modes in the dawn sector, are key to forming duct-favorable structures. The preferred region of ULF-controlled ducting is interpreted as the overlap between (i) MLT sectors where toroidal-mode ULF oscillations are efficiently excited and (ii) regions where chorus free energy is supplied by injected anisotropic electrons.

presentations.presentation_title: Microstructures in Magnetic Islands driven by Kinetic Instabilities in Collisionless Magnetic Reconnections
presentations.abstract: In collisionless magnetic reconnection, magnetic energy is released through a variety of processes. Inside magnetic islands, various microscopic instabilities driven by reconnection outflows are known to occur. Previous two-dimensional simulations have reported magnetic field fluctuations along the current sheet inside magnetic islands, and their origin has been discussed in terms of the Weibel instability. However, the fact that these fluctuations possess a wave number in the outflow direction cannot be explained by the Weibel instability, leaving their origin unresolved.In this study, we reexamine the magnetic field fluctuations observed inside magnetic islands. We explicitly consider the effect of electron magnetization caused by the weak magnetic field inside the island current sheet. Using magnetic islands reproduced by two-dimensional PIC simulations, we extract plasma parameters in the regions where the fluctuations are observed and perform additional simulations with an enlarged domain based on these parameters. By investigating the spatial structure of the fluctuations, their k–ω spectra, and the growth rates of the wave modes, and comparing them with the linear dispersion relations, we find that the magnetic field fluctuations inside magnetic islands can be understood as the oblique electron firehose instability.

presentations.presentation_title: Role of Field-line Curvature Scattering in Magnetosphere–ionosphere Coupling
presentations.institution: The University of Texas at Arlington
presentations.abstract: The nightside transition region between Earth’s magnetotail and the inner magnetosphere is characterized by strong precipitation of energetic electrons into the ionosphere. These electrons are scattered by electromagnetic whistler-mode and ion cyclotron waves, as well as by field-line curvature scattering (FLCS). In this presentation, we focus specifically on the latter mechanism, which primarily operates when the magnetotail current sheet, characterized by stretched magnetic field lines, penetrates into the outer radiation belt. We briefly review recent results on the efficiency of FLCS in governing outer radiation belt dynamics and then focus on the effects of precipitating electrons on ionospheric ionization. We compare several events in which low-altitude observations from ELFIN and DMSP cover a wide energy range of precipitating electrons, allowing separation between whistler-driven precipitation and precipitation caused by FLCS. We evaluate ionospheric density perturbations and show that precipitation due to FLCS can significantly enhance ionization at altitudes around 100 km and below. Finally, we discuss the possible collocation of the FLCS region with Region 2 field-aligned currents.

presentations.presentation_title: Excitation of Storm-time Pc5 Ulf Waves During the 22 July 2009 Storm: Comparison of Goes, Ground Observations, and Gemsis Coupled Simulation
presentations.abstract: Pc5 ultra-low-frequency (ULF) waves play a key role in the dynamics of ring current ions and radiation belt electrons through wave–particle interactions. However, where and how storm-time Pc5 waves are generated by ring current ions remain under debate. Yamakawa et al. (2022) investigated the excitation of two types of storm-time Pc5 waves using the GEMSIS magnetosphere–ionosphere coupled model. However, their simulation was performed under simplified and static Region-1 field-aligned current (FAC) and nightside ion injection. The purpose of this study is to investigate the excitation of Pc5 ULF waves during a magnetic storm under time-varying Region-1 FAC and time-dependent nightside ion injection. We focus on the 22 July 2009 magnetic storm and compare simulation results with a previous ring current model (CRCM; Fok et al., 2001) and spacecraft observations. During this event, Dst decreased to nearly −80 nT at 07:00 UT. The excitation of ULF waves was investigated using the GEMSIS coupled model (GEMSIS-RC and GEMSIS-POT), GOES satellites, and ground observations. GEMSIS-RC model is a drift-kinetic and self-consistent model for ring current ions, while GEMSIS-POT is a 2-D ionospheric potential solver. Poloidal Pc5 waves were observed by GOES and ground stations from 02:50 to 03:40 UT in the premidnight sector with wave frequency of 1.3–1.8 mHz and the azimuthal wave number of m ~ −5, indicating westward propagation. Pc5 waves are also generated in the model in the premidnight region, with similar frequency and m numbers to the observations. The simulation suggests that the waves are excited by drift resonance with 50–200 keV ring current ions and inward gradient of ion phase space density contributes to wave growth. These results demonstrate that the coupled model can connect time-dependent nightside injection to storm-time Pc5 excitation and its global distribution.

presentations.presentation_title: Formation of Spectral Gap of Chorus Emissions Around Half Electron Gyrofrequency Via Landau Resonance
presentations.abstract: Whistler-mode chorus waves are frequently detected in the Earth’s inner magnetosphere and are known for exhibiting a spectral gap around half of the electron gyrofrequency (0.5 fce). The formation mechanism of this spectral gap has not yet been fully understood, despite being widely reported in observations. Previous studies have suggested that nonlinear wave damping associated with Landau resonance plays a key role when chorus waves propagate obliquely away from the geomagnetic equator. Satellite observations by Geotail [1] and supporting test-particle simulations [2] have indicated that chorus waves, generated with a broad frequency spectrum near the equatorial region, undergo nonlinear wave damping around 0.5 fce at higher magnetic latitudes.In the present work, we investigate this nonlinear damping process using a self-consistent two-dimensional general curvilinear particle-in-cell (2D gcPIC) simulation. The simulation results clearly reproduce the spectral gap in slightly oblique chorus emissions, in agreement with observational characteristics. A detailed analysis of wave-particle interactions demonstrates that the damping is governed by nonlinear Landau resonance between chorus waves and energetic electrons. We further show that efficient energy transfer from the wave to electrons occurs under a stationary wave condition, in which the electron parallel velocity simultaneously matches the parallel phase velocity and group velocity of chorus waves. Based on this condition, we examine the relationship between chorus wave normal angles and wave frequencies, providing new insights into the spectral structure and propagation characteristics of chorus emissions. presentations.presentation_title: An Event Study on Persistent Emic Waves in the Dayside Magnetosphere During the Storm Recovery Phase
presentations.abstract: Electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves play an important role in regulating energetic particle fluxes in the Earth’s inner magnetosphere. In this presentation, we show an event study of persistent EMIC waves observed by the Van Allen Probes and the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission near local noon. The EMIC wave lasted for about three days during the late recovery phase of a geomagnetic storm, under steady solar wind dynamic pressure. During this interval, the EMIC waves intermittently disappeared and reappeared as the satellites traversed nearly the same region. We present an overview of this event and discuss possible generation and modulation mechanisms, including particle injections from the nightside and the presence of a plasmaspheric plume, which may contribute to the persistence and recurrence of the observed EMIC waves.

presentations.presentation_title: Mesospheric Plasma Trail Produced by Continuous Fragmentation of an Apollo-type Meteoroid
presentations.institution: Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Most meteoroids fragment during atmospheric entry, but the processes associated with continuous fragmentation and the formation of their plasma trail remain insufficiently understood. Here, we present observations of a slow meteoroid recorded at 18:30:10 UTC on 24 December 2022 by the meteor and ionospheric irregularity observation system (MIOS) in Hainan, China. The meteoroid entered the atmosphere with an initial velocity of 13.23 km/s and produced continuous luminous emission for more than 15 s over an altitude range of 81.0-41.1 km. This event exhibited multi-stage, non-explosive fragmentation accompanied by visible debris and gradual deceleration. Orbital analysis indicates a probable origin from an Apollo-type asteroid. The meteor is primarily composed of fragile and comet-like materials, but also contains regions with mechanical strengths comparable to carbonaceous meteorites, presenting significant internal heterogeneity due to variations in fragmentation resistance. Emission spectra further reveal a relatively homogeneous composition with a high sodium content. Accompanied by the meteoroid fragmentation, two non-field-aligned plasma irregularity structures were detected in the lower mesosphere at altitudes of approximately 64–60 km. We propose that continuous fragmentation releases dust particles that rapidly acquire electric charge, diffuse, and organize into Bragg-scale structures, producing the observed radar echoes. These observations suggest that continuous meteoroid fragmentation and associated dust charging processes may constitute an important mechanism for plasma structure formation in the mesosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Tracing the Origin of Daytime Ionospheric Topside Irregularities at Low Latitudes
presentations.institution: Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: While most equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs) dissipate before/around sunrise, some can persist into daytime in the topside ionosphere. Whereas the daytime F region topside irregularities are not a rare phenomenon, their origin is still not demonstrated. Using measurements from the Meteor and ionospheric Irregularity Observation System (MIOS) and ground-based Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers, cases of daytime ionospheric topside irregularities observed at low latitudes in China under both geomagnetic storm and quiet conditions are presented. By using the rate of change of total electron content index (ROTI) from GNSS receivers and plasma zonal drifts from the Equatorial ionospheric Zonal Plasma Drifts (EZDrifts) model, the origins of these daytime ionospheric topside irregularities were well identified. The results show that the daytime topside irregularities could originate from the EPBs generated on the previous night at the same, western or eastern longitudes. One interesting finding is that EPBs could first be detected by the radar during nighttime, their remnants could return to the radar site during daytime and be detected by radar once again on some occasions. Possible factors responsible for the long duration of EPB irregularities were discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Neutral Density Estimation Using the Ctipe Model and Data Assimilation
presentations.abstract: An accurate representation of the thermosphere-ionosphere is essential for a multitude of space weather applications. Actual measurements are sparse, limited to specific data types and with poorly defined uncertainties. Numerical models are often used as a substitute, sometimes in conjunction with data assimilation schemes.Recently, the physics-based Coupled Thermosphere Ionosphere Plasmasphere electrodynamics (CTIPe) model has been shown to provide accurate global estimates of neutral density when used in conjunction with the Thermosphere Ionosphere Data Assimilation scheme (TIDA). This approach adds the model inputs to the state vector and results in better accounting for the strongly forced nature of the TI.In this study, we expand on previous work by demonstrating the use of TIDA-CTIPe for neutral density estimation over a time interval of 10 years, covering multiple geomagnetic events and satelite missions (CHAMP, GRACE, GRACE-FO, SWARM) Aditionally, we demonstrate the possibility of improving neutral density by assimilating ionospheric measurements, such as slant-TEC measurements from COSMIC-2. Also, the importance of proper uncertainty for measurements is discussed, as well as the impact of potential biases on model result quality.Finally, we discuss several recent improvements and updates to the model in preparation for real-time operations. The need and potential usefuleness of real-time data sources for operations is discussed.

presentations.presentation_title: Long-term Statistical Analysis of Ionospheric Parameter for Forecasting HF Blackouts
presentations.abstract: Shortwave fadeouts (SWF) are sudden disruptions of high-frequency (HF) radio communication caused by enhanced solar X-ray emission during flares. Conventionally, the magnitude of SWF is estimated empirically based on the peak solar X-ray flux and the solar zenith angle. However, this flare-centric approach often fails to accurately predict the severity of ionospheric absorption, particularly in distinguishing between simple absorption enhancements and complete blackouts. Recent observations have highlighted those ionospheric conditions before flare, such as negative storms, critically modulate the impact of flares.This study proposes a new ionospheric susceptibility parameter, f B , defined as the ratio of the background F2-layer critical frequency (foF2) to the difference between foF2 and the minimum frequency (f min ). We performed a comprehensive statistical analysis using a long-term dataset spanning over 40 years (1981–2023) from four ionosonde stations in Japan.The results reveal that f B exhibits distinct seasonal and diurnal variations independent of the solar cycle, quantifying the background ionosphere's vulnerability to blackouts. We found that a high f B value significantly lowers the flare intensity threshold required to trigger a blackout. By incorporating f B into a new empirical model, the accuracy of blackout prediction improved significantly, with the Area Under the Curve (AUC) increasing from 0.75 to 0.82 compared to conventional methods. These findings demonstrate that monitoring f B enables real-time, pre-flare risk assessment, providing a robust foundation for improving operational space weather forecasting.

presentations.presentation_title: Automatic 3D Reconstruction of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) Based on Coronagraph Observations and Machine Learning Techniques
presentations.abstract: Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) are the major driver of severe space weather events, causing substantial economic losses to space-based and ground-based assets of human. It is essential to advance our understanding of CME propagation dynamics for better predictions. We have developed an algorithm that automatically reconstruct CME structure integrating dual-viewpoint observations with machine learning techniques. It consists of three stages: (1) region acquisition, (2) model construction, and (3) function optimization.A statistical analysis on more than 100 CME events is conducted to investigate both the two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) parameters. According to our statistics, the actual velocities are underestimated , and the widths are overestimated because of the projection effect from 2D observations. The proposed method can further be used to provide CME initial parameters for magnetohydrodynamics simulations, enabling a deeper understanding of CME kinematics.

presentations.presentation_title: A Framework for Developing Multi-perspective Prediction Models of Solar Energetic Particle Events
presentations.institution: Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute
presentations.abstract: It is known that a significant portion of the energy released during solar eruptive events such as flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) can be transferred to accelerate particles in the solar atmosphere and interplanetary space. These solar energetic particles (SEPs) then propagate into the heliosphere presumably guided by interplanetary magnetic field lines, and some of them may be observed in-situ as SEP events by particle detectors onboard satellites in various Earth orbits. Here we present the design and implementation of a framework that can be used not only for developing multi-perspective prediction models of earth-directed SEP events but also for investigating the origin of SEPs observed at Earth. An example of how this framework can be employed in space weather applications will be demonstrated, with a particular focus on deep learning models developed for: (1) predicting whether an SEP event, classified according to its peak proton flux at energies greater than 10 MeV, will occur for a target prediction interval (e.g., 12 hours), and (2) providing information on event characteristics, such as onset time and peak flux, in cases where an event is predicted to occur.

presentations.presentation_title: Investigation on Solar Wind Characteristic Parameters Using IPS Observations and PFSS+SCS Magnetic Field Extrapolations
presentations.abstract: Understanding the acceleration mechanisms of the solar wind is important not only for heliophysics, but also for practical applications such as space weather forecasting. Due to computational constraints, current operational space weather models widely employ semi-empirical approaches, in which the wind speed is predicted by characteristic parameters calculated from coronal magnetic-field extrapolations. Representative examples include the magnetic flux-tube expansion factor f SS (Wang & Sheeley 1990; Arge & Pizzo 2000), its ratio to the magnetic field strength at the coronal base f SS /B cb (Fujiki+ 2015) and distance from coronal hole boundary (DCHB, Arge+ 2004). To evaluate parameters applicable to a wide range of solar wind streams, observations at high latitudes–where fast wind is predominant–are particularly important. However, such available observations are limited. Interplanetary scintillation (IPS) observations (Kojima & Kakinuma 1990) provide one of the few such observations but have primarily relied on magnetic-field extrapolations based on the potential field source surface (PFSS) model. Since the PFSS model alone has limitations in reproducing latitudinal magnetic-field structures (Schatten 1971), combining it with the Schatten current sheet (SCS) model may improve the consistency with IPS-derived speed maps.In this study, we systematically investigate correlations between the wind speed derived from IPS observations and several magnetic parameters by combining IPS observations with PFSS+SCS model for 32 Carrington rotations. We find that f SS shows only a weak correlation with the wind speed, whereas f SS /B cb clearly separates the solar wind into two populations: one exhibiting a strong negative correlation and the other showing a weak positive correlation. This classification can be organized by the footpoint magnetic-field strength and DCHB. These results suggest the potential to improve the accuracy of semi-empirical models for wind speed and may also indicate the differences in underlying solar wind acceleration mechanisms.

presentations.presentation_title: Solar Wind Simulation Based on Neural Network Operators
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Efficient and accurate modeling of solar wind structures is essencial for investigating the propagation of solar storms and forecasting space weather. Although traditional three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) solar wind numerical models are physically self-consistent, their high computational cost limits their applicability for real-time space weather prediction. This study proposes a machine learning methodology based on neural network operators, which utilizes numerical simulation data to train neural network operators consistent with MHD theory, enabling efficient prediction of interplanetary solar wind conditions. Taking boundary conditions at 0.1 AU as input, the model outputs key physical fields of interplanetary solar wind, including velocity, density, temperature, and magnetic field. Supervised training using extensive MHD simulation data enables the neural network operators to learn the structural evolution of the solar wind. Validation reveals that the proposed model achieves a prediction speed two orders of magnitude faster than conventional numerical models. Experiments conducted over different Carrington rotations confirm that the model effectively captures structural features such as co-rotating interaction regions (CIRs) and agree with in-situ observations. These results demonstrate the potential of neural network operators for efficient modeling of the solar wind.

presentations.presentation_title: CLIP-Based Daily Space Weather Summary Generation from SDO Solar Images
presentations.abstract: Recent advances in vision–language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in image and video captioning tasks across diverse domains. However, their applicability to scientific solar observation data, particularly for automated generation of daily space weather summaries, remains insufficiently explored. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness of a CLIP-based vision–language model for generating daily space weather summaries from solar image time series.We analyze solar image sequences acquired by the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), focusing on major space weather–relevant phenomena such as solar flares, coronal holes, and active regions. Rather than applying CLIP to all video frames, we introduce a sparsity-aware frame reduction strategy that exploits the sparse intensity characteristics of solar image sequences. This approach enables efficient selection of representative frames for downstream caption generation while reducing computational cost. Based on the selected frames, we generate frame-level captions using a CLIP-based model fine-tuned on a curated dataset of SDO solar images. Captions describing solar flares, coronal holes, and active regions are aggregated and reorganized into a coherent daily space weather summary using a T5-based large language model. The generated summary not only describes solar activity but also includes inferred implications for geospace conditions, such as potential geomagnetic disturbances. The proposed framework is conceptualized as a data-mining model for sparse solar video sequences, enabling automated extraction, integration, and summarization of space weather–relevant information into concise daily summaries. Experiments using SDO data show that the proposed sparsity-aware pipeline reduces daily processing time from several minutes to a few seconds while preserving scientifically meaningful daily space weather summaries.

presentations.presentation_title: Operational CME Arrival and Magnetic Field Prediction with SUSANOO-CME
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
presentations.abstract: Predicting the arrival of Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs) and the southward magnetic field they bring remains a central challenge in operational space weather forecasting. To address this, we developed the global MHD model SUSANOO-CME (Shiota & Kataoka 2016), which simulates CME propagation including internal magnetic flux ropes. Building on this model, we recently established an operational prediction system that automatically sets model inputs using real-time solar observations. The system is fully operated through a web-based interface, enabling forecasters without computational expertise to run simulations, and automatically visualizes predicted solar wind and magnetic field conditions at Earth. This system has been in operational use at NICT since August 2022. We applied the system to four exceptionally intense solar storm events—May 2024, October 2024, November 2025, and January 2026. These events exhibited distinct CME structures and propagation behaviors, resulting in varied prediction performance. In two events, CMEs erupted in close succession; the earlier eruptions significantly modified the heliospheric environment, creating pre-conditioning that affected the propagation of the following CME. Such CME–CME interaction influenced shock evolution, solar wind speed and density, and the development of embedded flux ropes. In the remaining two events, the ambient background solar wind played a more dominant role in controlling CME propagation. These comparisons demonstrate that prediction accuracy depends not only on representing CME magnetic structures but also on reproducing background solar wind conditions and pre-conditioning by preceding eruptions. In this presentation, we introduce the SUSANOO-CME operational prediction system and assess its performance across these four major events. By contrasting successful and challenging aspects of the predictions, we highlight the current status of real-time CME forecasting and discuss future improvements in modeling background solar wind, CME–CME interaction, and magnetic field prediction.

presentations.presentation_title: The Solar Maximum of Solar Cycle 26: a Forecast Based on a White Noise Stochastic Process with Memory
presentations.abstract: The greatest solar activity occurs during the solar maximum where there is a reversal of the sun’s magnetic north and south poles accompanied by large solar storms, increased solar flares and coronal mass ejections. This heightened activity during a solar maximum can result in intense space weather, and disruptions to satellites, power grids, and radio communications. Predictions of when a solar maximum occurs within a solar cycle (SC) widely varies and have always been a scientifically difficult problem. We are now in SC 25 which is expected to end in 2030 to be followed by SC 26. In this work, a forecast of when the solar maximum for SC 26 will occur is made based on a white noise stochastic process with memory. This stochastic formulation was also used to forecast the solar maximum of the current SC 25 by Toledo et al (Physica Scripta 2024; DOI:10.1088/1402-4896/ad7207) with good agreement with the observed solar maximum. Data for the daily sunspot numbers (SSN) for solar cycles 10 to 25 were obtained from the World Data Center SILSO Observatory (https://www.sidc.be/SILSO/datafiles). We detrended the fluctuations by subtracting a 9-day moving average from the original daily SSN values. The method utilizes only the first four years of each solar cycle where the mean square deviation (MSD) of the detrended daily SSN is evaluated. Matching the theoretical MSD of the model with the MSD of the SSN gives values of the decay parameter beta for each solar cycle. A theoretical prediction of the time of occurrence of a solar maximum is obtained as a function of a transformed beta. This gives the predicted solar maximum for SC 26 to be 4.32 years from the start of SC 26 with uncertainty of 4 months.

presentations.presentation_title: Earthquake Precursor Signals - Need of Satellite Mission
presentations.institution: International Research Center for Space and Planetary environment Science
presentations.abstract: The presentation is to report our findings of ionosphere modification about the precursor phenomena of large earthquakes larger than about M≥6.8 in Japan. At the initial part of my talk, we show the findings of the maximum electron density, NmF 2 which were acquired every 15 min by 4 ionosonde stations in Japan (NICT), and tilting of the ground surface observed at many stations (NIED) in Japan. Height profile of neutral temperature up to 120 Km, which is acquired by an instrument, SARBAR installed in TIMED satellite. We describe the case of Tohoku-Oki earthquake which occurred on March 11 2011, as one of the typical examples. NmF2 (maximum electron density in the ionosphere) shows especially the minimum or maximum 5 days before the earthquake depending on the ionosonde location. The similar pattern is found for the NmF2 for Sichuan Earthquake in Main land China (May12, 2008,7.9-8.3 M, and Chi-Chi earthquake in Taiwan (21 September 1999, Mw 7.6). Slant gauge which detects the tilting of the ground surface at the place where the sensor is located shows the unique behavior starting from about 2 weeks before the earthquake. Height profile of atmospheric temperature shows the small increase around the height of 45 km, 5 days before and the irregularities of Tn extends to the height of 120 km. So far, we studied 6 earthquakes occurred in Japan. All earthquakes shows the same features of ground motion and NmF2. At the last of my talk, I would like to stress the need of satellite constellation, which hopefully should be conducted as an international project, especially among Asian countries.

presentations.presentation_title: Zonal Wind at the E region with High Pedersen Conductivity Modulate F-region Plasma Density Over Asian-pacific Region
presentations.abstract: Longitudinal wave-3 and wave-4 structures in the ionosphere and the neutral atmosphere have been widely studied over the past two decades. However, pronounced differences exist between the global longitudinal peak structures in the ionosphere and those in the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT), which remain poorly understood. To investigate these differences, we analyze the plasma density from the Global Ionospheric Specification (GIS) and neutral winds from the Ionospheric Connection Explorer (ICON). Results indicate that uniquely strong eastward winds in the lower thermosphere (above 126 km) over the Asian and Pacific sectors can drive eastward plasma drifts in the F region. This process contributes to the plasma density peaks in these two regions and consequently leads to the globally uneven longitudinal distribution of ionospheric structures.

presentations.presentation_title: A Simple Index for Estimating Tec Disturbance Amplitudes Based on Acoustic Ray Geometry
presentations.abstract: The widespread availability of TEC measurements has enabled two-dimensional observations of various ionospheric phenomena, rather than observations limited to isolated points, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of ionospheric dynamics. Phenomena such as medium-scale traveling ionospheric disturbances (MSTIDs), ionospheric disturbances following earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, and rocket-induced disturbances can be effectively investigated using TEC observations. However, a fundamental limitation of TEC is that it does not provide altitude-specific information, as it represents an integrated plasma density along the signal path. TEC measurements are often assumed to primarily reflect plasma density variations near the ionospheric F2 peak altitude, allowing the geographic locations of disturbances to be inferred. Nevertheless, several studies have reported results suggesting that TEC measurements also capture disturbances occurring at other altitudes (e.g., Maeda and Heki, 2013; Kakinami et al., 2013, 2021). In addition, the integration of positive and negative perturbations along the ray path can lead to an apparent cancellation, resulting in the non-detection of actual disturbances. Consequently, simple analyses may lead to misinterpretations of the underlying physical processes. In this study, we investigated TEC disturbances following the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake, the 2024 Hyuga-nada earthquake, and the 2026 offshore Aomori earthquake. We calculated the ray paths of acoustic waves emitted from the epicenters using Hamiltonian equations in spherical coordinates, and examined both the angles between the acoustic wave propagation directions and the geomagnetic field, and the angles between the propagation directions and the TEC observation geometry. Based on these parameters, we established a simple index for estimating TEC disturbance amplitudes. The proposed index shows good agreement with the observed amplitude distributions of TEC disturbances for all three earthquakes. In this presentation, we introduce this index and discuss its applicability.

presentations.presentation_title: Climatology of Equatorial Plasma Bubbles: Role of Gravity Wave Seeding and Ionospheric Preconditioning
presentations.abstract: This study investigates the linkage between mesopause gravity waves and equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs) from 2012-2015 using the collocated nightglow measurements, O 2 (762nm) and OI (630 nm), observed by the Visible and near-Infrared Spectral Imager onboard the International Space Station under the Ionosphere, Mesosphere, upper Atmosphere, and Plasmasphere (ISS-IMAP/VISI) mission, along with the ionospheric observations from FORMOSAT-3/COSMIC (F3/C). ISS-IMAP/VISI observed a persistent three-peak longitudinal structure of gravity wave activity near the magnetic equator in South American, African, and South Asian sectors across all seasons. The gravity waves also exhibit significant seasonal latitudinal variations, consistent with the seasonal migration of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ). Notably, the longitudinal distribution of gravity wave occurrences aligns well with the longitudinal pattern of EPB occurrence observed by both VISI and F3/C, particularly over the South American-African sectors, establishing that ITCZ-driven gravity waves are the potential seeding source for EPBs. Analysis of ionospheric background conditions relevant to Rayleigh-Taylor instability confirms that while these conditions strongly influence the seasonal-longitudinal distribution of EPBs, the presence of gravity waves supports the gravity wave seeding hypothesis. Overall, the VISI EPB occurrence rates are consistent with the product of VISI gravity wave and favorable background condition occurrence probabilities, demonstrating that the climatology of EPBs is synergistically governed by the gravity wave seeding and ionospheric conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Observations of Lithosphere-atmosphere-ionosphere Coupling Induced by Diverse Geophysical Events
presentations.abstract: This paper presents recent multi-instrumental observational results investigating the mechanisms of Lithosphere-Atmosphere-Ionosphere (LAI) coupling. We analyze three distinct types of geophysical phenomena: (1) earthquakes, (2) volcanic eruptions, and (3) tropical cyclones (TCs). The University of Electro-Communications (UEC) maintains an extensive electromagnetic observation suite across Japan, including a dense VLF/LF transmitter signal network to monitor lower ionospheric perturbations (D and E regions). These data are integrated with lightning data from the Japanese Total Lightning Network (JTLN) connecting to ENTLN, atmospheric electric field (AEF) measurements, and IR sensor data from the Himawari-8 satellite. Notably, our analysis identifies Internal Gravity Waves (IGWs) as a dominant component of the atmospheric gravity waves (AGWs) excited during geophysical phenomena. By synthesizing these multi-instrumental datasets, this study identifies unique ionospheric signatures originating from lithospheric and atmospheric sources, providing new insights into the vertical coupling processes during extreme geophysical events.

presentations.presentation_title: Ionospheric Responses to Natural Hazards and Anthropogenic Activities by Using Ground- and Space-based Gnss Measurements
presentations.abstract: Ionospheric plasma density distribution often responds to the energy released during lithospheric and lower atmospheric processes, variations related to solar and geomagnetic conditions, as well as the result of man-made activities. The lithospheric and atmospheric processes include natural hazards such as earthquakes, volcano eruptions, tsunami propagation, and severe weather systems. Geomagnetic storms are another major source of external forcing that produce large-scale variations in plasma density as well as trigger the generation of plasma irregularities that could severely impact satellite communication and navigation. The man-made activities include the ionospheric variations related to rocket and missile launches, nuclear explosions, etc. Understanding the impacts of such external energy input on the plasma density distribution requires regular monitoring of the background ionosphere with higher spatial and temporal resolutions. This study examines the application of Global Ionospheric Specification (GIS) 3D electron density profiles constructed by using GNSS-RO total electron content measurements in investigating such ionospheric responses. The results will focus on the ionospheric observations by using GIS during (1) the ionosphere plasma density holes created by rockets launched on consecutive days in January 2024, (2) persisting plasma bubble observations following the 01 December 2023 geomagnetic storm, and (3) the ionospheric perturbations and plasma irregularities triggered following the Tonga volcano eruption on 15 January 2022.

presentations.presentation_title: Enhancing Geospace Dynamics Constellation (GDC) Science: Ephemeris Validation and Kamodo-powered Data Visualization
presentations.institution: The Catholic University of America/ NASA GSFC
presentations.abstract: The upcoming Geospace Dynamics Constellation (GDC) mission is poised to revolutionize our understanding of magnetosphere-ionosphere-thermosphere coupling through multi-point observations. Maximizing the scientific return from such a complex, distributed mission critically depends on optimized sampling and intuitive, robust data analysis and visualization tools. This study addresses these foundational requirements for GDC. We present research focused on the optimization of GDC's ephemerides/constellation evolution and the development of advanced data visualization capabilities using the Kamodo suite of tools. We work with the simulated GDC ephemeris, retrieving the six satellite positions during their orbits around the Earth during the 4 phases of the mission. Concurrently, we leverage Kamodo to create synthetic data sets from ionosphere-thermosphere models, and develop dynamic and insightful visualizations and analyses of these synthetic datasets. This includes interactive representations of the constellation's relative configurations.We demonstrate how these tools facilitate the analysis of spatial conjunctions, the temporal evolution of geospace phenomena along specific flight paths, and the overall constellation dynamics, providing a powerful framework for mission planning and scientific discovery through an accessible framework for data exploration, serving as a valuable paradigm for future multi-spacecraft investigations in geospace and beyond.

presentations.presentation_title: Validation of Icon-derived Ionospheric Currents Using Ohm’s Law and Esa Swarm Magnetometer Data
presentations.abstract: The equatorial ionosphere undergoes significant daily variations, partly driven by lower thermospheric neutral winds that generate currents through the neutral wind dynamo process. NASA’s Ionospheric Connection Explorer (ICON) enables simultaneous space-based observations of thermospheric neutral winds and ionospheric electric fields through in situ plasma drift measurements near the magnetic equator. By combining conductivities, neutral wind, and electric field data, ionospheric currents can be calculated. During conjunctions with the European Space Agency’s Swarm satellites, magnetic signatures of ionospheric currents are measured by Swarm. These measurements reveal a moderate to strong correlation, with a correlation coefficient of approximately 0.5, between the zonal currents derived from ICON (J ICON ) and the eastward component of the Sq current system derived from Swarm’s magnetic observations (J SWARM ) near local noon. However, J ICON is approximately five times larger than J SWARM . This discrepancy is puzzling because ionospheric current estimates should be consistent regardless of the observation or retrieval method. One likely source of uncertainty is the conductivity used in the J ICON calculation, which must be estimated using models due to the lack of direct observation. This study examines the mismatch between J ICON and J SWARM from two complementary perspectives: (1) the extent to which measurement uncertainties contribute to the discrepancy, and (2) the conductivity profiles required to reconcile J ICON and J SWARM ​ in a one-to-one relationship.

presentations.presentation_title: Loading of Relativistic Maxwellian-type Distributions Revisited
presentations.abstract: A simple numerical method for loading of a relativistic Maxwellian-type distribution is proposed based on inverse transform sampling. The relativistic Maxwellian energy distribution is introduced as an alternative to the Maxwell-Juttner distribution. The cumulative distribution of the shifted-Maxwellian energy distribution is approximated by an invertible function. Random variates of energy is transformed from uniformly distributed random variables. Then, the energy variates are converted to momentum vector variates. Numerical tests are presented to show that the present method successfully reproduce the relativistic Maxwellian energy distribution.

presentations.presentation_title: Shue et al. Magnetopause Models: Retrospects, Applications, and Future Prospects
presentations.abstract: The magnetopause is the outermost boundary of the magnetosphere. Its position is mainly determined by the solar wind dynamic pressure and the north-south component of the interplanetary magnetic field. The two sets of formulas by Shue et al. [1997; 1998] can well describe the changes of the Earth's magnetopause under stable and large-scale conditions. They used magnetopause crossing events to fit the parameters listed in the sets of formulas. These sets of formulas have been widely accepted by Space Physicists and have become the standard model in the Space Physics community. This report will introduce the formulas used for fitting, the data used in the model construction, the similarities and differences between the sets of formulas proposed by Shue et al. At the same time, this paper will also mention the development history of these models and the criticisms they received before and after the implementation of the magnetopause project. These two models have a wide range of applications, including estimations of parameters related to the magnetopause, magnetosheath, and bow shock. These results can be compared with the output from global magnetospheric models. These models produce the boundary conditions for the Tsyganenko empirical global magnetospheric model and the VERB-4D numerical inner magnetospheric model. Their applications also include the study of other planets and the Moon, even the exosphere and stratosphere of planets. Finally, some potential future research directions will be pointed out in this presentation. References: [1] Shue, J.-H., et al. (1997). A new functional form to study the solar wind control of the magnetopause size and shape. Journal of Geophysical Research, 102(A5), 9497–9511. https://doi.org/10.1029/97JA00196; [2] Shue, J. H., et al. (1998). Magnetopause location under extreme solar wind conditions. Journal of Geophysical Research, 103(A8), 17691–17700. https://doi.org/10.1029/98JA01103

presentations.presentation_title: Properties of Current Sheets in 2D Tearing-Mediated MHD Turbulence
presentations.abstract: It is well known that the nonlinear evolution of MHD turbulence generates intermittent current sheets. In the solar wind turbulence, current sheets are frequently observed and they are believed to be an important pathway for the turbulence energy to dissipate and heat the plasma. In this study, we perform a comprehensive analysis of current sheets in a high-resolution two-dimensional simulation of balanced, incompressible MHD turbulence. The simulation parameters are selected such that tearing mode instability is triggered and plasmoids are generated throughout the simulation domain. We develop an automated method to identify current sheets and accurately quantify their key parameters including thickness (a), length (L), and Lundquist number (S). Before the triggering of tearing instability, the current sheet lengths are mostly comparable to the energy injection scale. After the tearing mode onsets, smaller current sheets with lower Lundquist numbers are generated. We find that the aspect ratio (a/L) of the current sheets scales approximately as S -1/2 , i.e. the Sweet-Parker scaling. While a power-law scaling between L and a is observed, no clear correlation is found between the upstream magnetic field strength and thickness a. Finally, although the turbulence energy shows anisotropy between the directions parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field increment, we do not observe a direct correspondence between the shape of the current sheets and that of the turbulence "eddies." These results suggest that one needs to be cautious when applying the scale-dependent dynamic alignment model to the analysis of current sheets in MHD turbulence.

presentations.presentation_title: Charge Sign Dependent Drift Effects in the Time Lag of Cosmic Ray Variation Relative to Solar Activity Observed with CALET
presentations.abstract: The 11-yr variation of galactic cosmic-ray flux lags behind the variation of the sunspot number. An average ~1-yr time-lag is expected from the outward propagating solar wind with the frozen-in photospheric magnetic field varying in the solar cycle, and from the inward diffusive transport of cosmic-ray particles. The long-term neutron monitor data, however, show that the time-lag is significantly longer (shorter) in the odd (even) solar cycle. In this paper, we analyze the time-lag in proton and electron fluxes observed by the CALET. It is found that the time-lag is similar in proton and electron fluxes during an A>0 polarity epoch of the solar dipole magnetic field. In an even solar cycle 24, including a polarity reversal from A<0 to A>0, on the other hand, it is found that the time-lag of proton (electron) flux variation is significantly shorter (longer) than the average ~1-yr lag by analyzing the combined data with CALET and AMS-02. This is the first observation of the charge-sign dependent time-lag. We demonstrate that these observations can be qualitatively interpreted in terms of different 11-yr time profiles of proton and electron fluxes in A>0 and A<0 epochs expected from the drift effect.

presentations.presentation_title: Fundamental Physical Processes of the Steady Solar Wind-magnetosphere System Under Northward Imf Conditions in the Framework of the Magnetic Topology
presentations.abstract: To understand the physical processes of the steady solar wind-magnetosphere system, two aspects must be considered: (i) the dynamical processes, which govern the distribution of mass, momentum, and energy, and (ii) the magnetic field topology, which governs the three-dimensional reconnection between the solar wind and the magnetosphere. Because the magnetic topology is determined by the combined interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and geomagnetic field, the solar wind and magnetosphere should be treated as a single magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid system. In this unified system, the physical processes can be interpreted as the interaction between the plasma and the magnetic field. When the plasma is absent, a vacuum magnetic-field configuration emerges, representing the system's ground state. Therefore, the dynamics of the system can be described as a balance between two forces: a force returning the magnetic field to its ground state and a force exerted by the solar wind plasma that deforms the magnetic field lines. This framework is referred to as the mechanical principle. The vacuum magnetic field exhibits a characteristic topology with two null points and two separators, which provide the magnetic framework for separator reconnection. Global MHD simulations have confirmed that this topology is preserved under northward IMF conditions, a property we refer to as the topology conservation property. Both the mechanical principle and the topology conservation property together determine the magnetic field structure of a quasi-steady solar wind-magnetosphere system. Therefore, this study achieves a fundamental understanding of the interaction between magnetic topology and plasma dynamics in the solar wind-magnetosphere system in the northward IMF conditions. Within this framework, we discussed that both the topology conservation property and the mechanical principle play essential roles in the formation of the steady-state magnetic field structure of the magnetotail and the plasma sheet in the northward IMF condition.

presentations.presentation_title: Automatic Detection and Quantitative Evaluation of Spread F Intensity Using Machine Learning
presentations.abstract: Spread F is a long-standing topic in ionospheric studies that hinders the identification of the key parameters from ionograms. Current automated scaling systems often misidentify these diffused echoes, leading to inaccurate readout parameters. This study proposes a two-stage approach to appropriately handle spread F data and improve the overall reliability of automated ionosonde observations. First, a pixel-level spread F detection method using Mask R-CNN, a deep learning-based instance segmentation model was developed. In validation with the ionogram at Shigaraki MU Observatory and one of the SEALION (South East Asia Low-latitude Ionospheric Network) ionosonde, the model achieved automated spread F detection with over 92% accuracy. Second, a scoring method was developed to quantitatively evaluate the degree of disturbance based on physical features such as echo area and height. This was motivated by cases in low-latitude SEALION data where binary classification (presence/absence) was insufficient. Multi-dimensional features were compressed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and their central trajectory was estimated as a principal curve. By defining this curve as a one-dimensional axis representing the degree of disturbance, objective scores based on the projection of each data are calculated. point onto this axis. The scores are highly correlated with manual assessments by experts, successfully distinguishing between severe and minor disturbances. This system enables the assignment of reliability flags to automatically scaled parameters, such as marking parameters as low-confidence when scores are high. This provides a critical metric for judging data validity and significantly contributes to the enhancement of automated ionospheric observation systems.
