presentations.presentation_title: A New Air Shower Array in the Southern Hemisphere: the Alpaca Experiment
presentations.institution: Institute for Cosmic ray research, University of Tokyo
presentations.abstract: The detection of sub-PeV γ rays from the Crab nebula by the Tibet ASγ collaboration opened a new window to search for the origins of cosmic rays in our Galaxy. Using the same technique as the Tibet experiment (surface array+underground water Cherenkov muon detector) we are building a new detector in the Southern Hemisphere: the Andes Large area PArticle detector for Cosmic ray physics and Astronomy (ALPACA).ALPACA is being installed at an altitude of 4740 m in the Chacaltaya plateau, Bolivia, covering an area of 83 000 m2 with 401 scintillation counters and 4 underground muons detectors (MDs). The prototype array called ALPAQUITA, having 1/4 of the total area of the ALPACA, started observations in September 2022. Moreover, ALPAQUITA is capable of observing lower energy cosmic rays by using counting rates of any 1 and any 2 scintillators in coincidence, opening the possibility to study solar-related phenomena like Forbush decreases (FDs).In this presentation we will show the current status of ALPAQUITA and the plans to extend the array, including the construction of the MDs. We will also report the results of the analysis of the initial data in the time period between 2023-2024, which includes a very important FD in May 2024. For this analysis we will compare compare our results with neutron monitors and muon detectors around world to study the rigidity dependence of these events, showing the capabilities of ALPACA/ALPAQUITA to study FDs at the highest rigidities.

presentations.presentation_title: ELF/VLF Wave Propagation in the Low-latitude Plasmasphere-Ionosphere
presentations.abstract: In the deep plasmasphere-ionosphere, plasma waves across a broad frequency range are often detected. Among them, we focus on two field-aligned wave modes, the whistler waves in the very-low-frequency (VLF: 3-30kHz) range and the electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves in the extremely-low-frequency (ELF: 3-300Hz) range. Right-handed polarized (RHP) whistler waves include artificially generated VLF signals, such as VLF communications, while left-handed polarized (LHP) or linearly polarized EMIC waves are naturally generated in space. In the deep plasmasphere, EMIC waves are suggested to be generated via mode conversion from incoming compressional waves (e.g., magnetosonic waves or equatorial noise) at the crossover location. At present, many numerical studies are limited to ray-tracing calculations to model these waves because the wavelength is much smaller than the wave path length. However, small-scale plasma density irregularities naturally occur; full-wave simulations are required to understand their properties. In this presentation, we conduct full-wave simulations of ELF/VLF waves in the deep plasmasphere-ionosphere. By adopting the Petra-M simulation tool and incorporating the GCPM and SAMI3 density models, we briefly demonstrate ELF/VLF wave properties, such as polarization and wave normal angle, from the source to the ground. As a result, we show that the wave normal angle changes dramatically as the wave propagates along the field line.

presentations.presentation_title: Development of Swirls in the Thermosphere and Ionosphere During the May 2024 Storm: GITM Simulation
presentations.abstract: In this study, we employed the Global Ionosphere Thermosphere Model to simulate the response of the ionosphere-thermosphere system to the May 2024 geomagnetic storm. The simulation revealed swirls in integrated O/N 2 (ΣO/N 2 ), temperature, and total electron contents. Based on the analysis of the simulation results, we conclude that two steps are necessary for the formation of swirls: (1) a vortex of winds formed at high latitudes due to two-cell convection pattern; (2) the vortex was advected to the lower latitudes by winds generated by JH.

presentations.presentation_title: Weird Aurora Over Svalbard
presentations.abstract: Fragmented aurora-like emissions are an ionospheric feature in the 557.7 nm emissions that were first reported in 2021 above Svalbard in the High Arctic (78 geographic degrees North). The fragments cannot be considered aurora in the conventional sense as they are not created by particle precipitation and are not field-aligned. They are small in scale (km), short-lived (minutes) and often periodically occurring, where individual fragments show dynamic internal structuring. Their cause is currently uncertain, but is an important mystery to solve as we believe they are visible manifestations of waves and turbulence that occur under strong electric fields. We present fragment observations manually identified from two years of Svalbard all-sky camera data, where AI was used to identify periods that were cloud-free and contained aurora. Triangulation techniques were applied to the fragments, which allows an estimation of the emission altitude. Fragments were frequently observed in close proximity to auroral arcs and seemed to move with them, suggesting a possible coupling between auroral precipitation-driven processes and aurora-like emissions. However, fragments were also observed during periods of weak or absent aurora. The relationship between fragments, local electric fields, and surrounding auroral activity remains an open question, with implications for our understanding of mesoscale electrodynamic coupling and energy transfer in the high-latitude ionosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: The Remarkable Response of Thermospheric Wind and Ion-neutral Coupling at Middle Latitudes During May 2024 Superstorm
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: This work investigates the nighttime thermospheric wind responses and Neutral-Ion coupling at east Asia during May 2024 Superstorm based on a multi-instrument dataset and NCAR-TIEGCM simulations. Remarkable equatorward wind surges were detected on the early storm stage of May 10, with the maximum speeds -438.45 m/s, -654 m/s and -398 m/s at geomagnetic latitudes 49°N, 39°N and 37°N, respectively, associated with a large-scale gravity wave. On May 11, the nighttime thermospheric winds shifted primarily to a strong westward flow, while remaining relatively weak in the meridional direction. Around geomagnetic latitudes 49°N, the eastward reversal of zonal winds and enhanced dawnside eastward ion drift after 18:00 UT on May 10, together with the strong westward winds and ion drifts on May 11 duskside, both pointed to potential ion-neutral coupling. TIEGCM successfully reproduced the nighttime thermospheric wind responses at east Asia but didn’t capture the variations of ion drift.

presentations.presentation_title: Short- and Long-term Variability of Upper Thermospheric Helium from Ground-based Optical Observations at Longyearbyen, Svalbard
presentations.abstract: This study investigates the temporal variability of metastable orthohelium, He(2 3 S), across multiple timescales in the polar region. The orthohelium layer is known to form between approximately 250 km and 800 km altitude, or even higher, making it a promising tracer for remote sensing of upper thermospheric and lower exospheric dynamics. However, variations in orthohelium associated with geomagnetic disturbances remain poorly understood. We analyzed a dataset of continuous He(2 3 S) airglow brightness at 1083 nm obtained during two recent winter seasons (2024–2025 and 2025–2026) using the short-wavelength infrared imaging spectrograph NIRAS-2 at the Kjell Henriksen Observatory (KHO), Svalbard (78.1°N, 16.0°E). The He(2³S) airglow time series exhibits clear seasonal variations, including the well-known helium winter bulge, as well as a pronounced dependence on solar zenith angle (SZA). We further examine He(2 3 S) variability as a function of SZA, magnetic local time (MLT), geomagnetic activity, and solar wind parameters. In addition, several episodes of sudden enhancements in He(2 3 S) airglow brightness were identified, likely associated with magnetic storms and solar proton events. These enhancements are interpreted as resulting from particle precipitation (He + /He ++ ions and electrons), and some of them were observed when KHO was located within the cusp region. Statistical analysis demonstrates that He(2 3 S) brightness fluctuations with time scale shorter than 6 hours have large amplitudes around 12 MLT. In the presentation, we will further discuss the results in detail.

presentations.presentation_title: Ionospheric Variations Observed at Syowa Station, Antarctica, During Large Space Weather Events Occurred in May and October 2024
presentations.institution: National Institute of Information and Communications Technology
presentations.abstract: The National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT) has conducted continuous ionospheric observations at Syowa Station, Antarctica, for more than 60 years. During Solar Cycle 25, the largest geomagnetic storm to date occurred in May 2024, followed by another major disturbance in October 2024. Analysis of ionosonde measurements and GNSS scintillation data at Syowa Station revealed three common features across both events: (1) disappearance of ionosonde echoes, (2) the occurrence of negative ionospheric storms, and (3) enhancement of phase scintillation. The echo blackouts were primarily attributed to enhanced ionospheric absorption driven by energetic particle precipitation. Comparison with particle data from GOES and POES satellites indicates that the October event was dominated by solar proton precipitation, whereas the May event involved both solar protons and auroral electrons in the 10s-100s keV range. Negative ionospheric storms were identified through reductions in foF 2 and total electron content (TEC), with occasional upward shift of high-altitude echoes during the recovery phase. Phase-scintillation enhancements coincided with irregular E-region structures, such as auroral-type and slanted sporadic-E layers, and notably persisted throughout the negative ionospheric storm intervals at Syowa Station—contrasting with reports of scintillation suppression in the polar region.

presentations.presentation_title: Superdarn Hop Radars - a Powerful Tool for Investigating the Interaction Between Geospace Plasma and Upper Atmosphere
presentations.abstract: Geospace plasmas are closely coupled with the neutral atmosphere in various ways. To understand detailed interaction mechanisms, it is crucial to use observation data with high spatial and temporal resolution and wide-area coverage. The Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN) is one of the few existing instruments that satisfy all the above criteria. In this paper, we present an overview, scientific achievements, and future perspectives of the SuperDARN Hokkaido Pair of (HOP) radars, which are operated by ISEE, Nagoya University, and are located at the lowest geomagnetic latitude (about 37 degrees) among the SuperDARN radars. We present selected results on ion-neutral interactions, such as Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances (TIDs) and coseismic ionospheric disturbances. We also introduce recent efforts to increase the temporal resolution of the data by up to 10x by implementing multi-beam capability.

presentations.presentation_title: Energy Transfer from Mhd-scale Slow-mode Waves to Kinetic-scale Ion Acoustic Waves
presentations.abstract: Large-amplitude slow-mode waves are commonly observed near Earth's magnetopause. Recent observations show that these waves can occur simultaneously with kinetic-scale ion acoustic waves. The amplitude of the ion acoustic waves is enhanced near the magnetic field peaks of the slow-mode wave, suggesting that the slow-mode waves may drive the generation of ion acoustic waves. To test this hypothesis, we conduct a hybrid simulation using observation-based parameters. The simulation results demonstrate that large-amplitude slow-mode waves generate counter-streaming ion beams, which in turn excite ion acoustic waves and relax the ion beams. Our study reveals a clear energy transfer channel from MHD-scale slow-mode waves to kinetic-scale ion acoustic waves.

presentations.presentation_title: MMS Observations of Multi-species Wave-particle Interactions and Rapid Foreshock Evolution
presentations.abstract: The ion foreshock is the region upstream of Earth’s bow shock where magnetic field lines connect to the quasi-parallel shock surface. Within this region, there exist a variety of backstreaming ion populations from the shock ramp that can generate ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves through wave-particle interactions. In this work, we use data from the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission to study such ULF waves and backstreaming ions during a prolonged interval of above-average solar wind helium abundance, embedded in a multi-day period of strong solar activity driven by a CME. When interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) orientations positioned MMS within the ion foreshock, the spacecraft captured the complete evolutionary sequence of the backstreaming ion velocity distributions: the initial formation of a reflected ion beam, followed by phase bunching and generation of coherent ULF waves, and eventual thermalization and randomization in velocity space to form diffuse ions. Intervals with elevated energetic He++ flux exhibited broadened and frequency-downshifted wave spectra, consistent with heavy-ion cyclotron resonance effects. The unusually rapid beam-to-diffuse transitions observed near the foreshock boundary likely result from the combined effects of multi-species wave-particle interactions and higher backstreaming ion densities during this active interval. These findings underscore the need for simulations and modeling that incorporate multi-species effects.

presentations.presentation_title: Shock Reformation Induced by Ion-scale Whistler Waves in Quasiperpendicular Bow Shock
presentations.abstract: Studies have long suggested that shocks can undergo cyclical self-reformation as a type of shock nonstationarity. Until now, providing solid evidence for shock reformation in spacecraft observation and identifying its generating mechanisms remain challenging. In this Letter, by analyzing magnetospheric multiscale observations, we unambiguously identified shock reformation occurring in a quasiperpendicular shock. A 2D PIC simulation reproduces and explains the observed shock reformation. The result reveals that the shock reformation is driven by the ion-scale whistler waves, manifested in two distinct types: whistler precursor and modified two-stream instability whistlers. An interesting finding is that the two mechanisms compete and dominate the reformation at early and later stages, respectively. Our results not only provide evidence of ion-scale whistlers as mechanism driving shock reformation, but also demonstrate the detailed kinetic processes how it happens, offering valuable insights into shock dynamics.

presentations.presentation_title: Investigating Properties of the Bow Shock Reflected Ions Using 2d Local Hybrid Simulations
presentations.abstract: Incoming solar wind ions can be reflected by Earth’s bow shock, and sometimes travel upstream and form a foreshock depending on the geometry between the background magnetic field and the bow shock. These reflected ions can further induce various perturbations and have important influence on the dayside interactions between the solar wind and Earth’s magnetosphere. Therefore, understanding the properties of the bow shock reflected ions and the detailed reflecting mechanisms is important for a complete comprehension of the dayside interactions and downstream dynamics. Based on the parameters of a real bow shock crossing event observed by THEMIS, we conduct a 2D local hybrid simulation of the bow shock to reveal the detailed ion dynamics at the bow shock. Our results show that the backstreaming ions upstream of bow shock are well-reproduced by the simulation. We further reveal the ion trajectories and kinetics at the bow shock by performing particle tracing in the simulation. Our findings include: (1) the high energy ions observed upstream of the shock in this simulation are generated by reflection instead of magnetosheath leakage; (2) the ions are accelerated by repeatedly crossing the shock and their energy gain approximately equals to the work done by the convection electric field, consistent with the Shock Drift Acceleration (SDA) process; (3) freshly reflected ions with larger initial pitch angles, higher initial kinetic energies, and velocity vectors pointing toward the downstream direction immediately prior to their first shock encounter are more likely to gain enough energy to escape the shock and become foreshock ions. Lastly, using particle tracing results, we discuss possible reasons for the differences between the observed and simulated reflected ion properties such as the discrepancy in reflection rate and ion energy spectrum.

presentations.presentation_title: Statistical Analysis of Hermean Foreshock Waves in the Intermediate and Whistler Frequency Range
presentations.abstract: The uniqueness of Mercury’s bow shock influences the interaction that occurs at this boundary and the types of ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves observed. Previous studies have reported 3 broad classification of waves observed at Mercury based on their characteristic frequencies and wave properties: (i) higher frequency; 2 Hz whistlers waves (similar to the 1 Hz waves at Earth), (ii) intermediate frequency of 0.8 Hz, whose properties and formation mechanism remains unknown, (iii) lower frequency, fast magnetosonic waves in the 0.05 – 0.4 Hz range (similar to the large amplitude 30-s waves observed in the Earth’s foreshock). This work presents an overview of the comprehensive statistical analysis of the properties of foreshock waves observed within the intermediate (0.6hz -0.9hz) and whistlers (1hz - 4 Hz) range upstream of the hermean bow shock using 4-years of magnetic field measurements from the magnetometer (MAG) instrument onboard the MESSENGER spacecraft. The identification was performed based on the waveform of each ULF wave as observed in the spectrogram using wavelet analysis. We report the characteristics (i.e. frequency and occurrence), foreshock conditions and properties of these waves (i.e. polarization) in the spacecraft frame using the minimum variance analysis (MVA) and discuss the probable generation mechanisms for waves in the intermediate frequency range.

presentations.presentation_title: Impacts of 3-second Waves on Earth's Foreshock Dynamics: Multi-case Study Observations
presentations.abstract: We presented magnetic field and plasma measurements of three case studies analyses of 3-seconds (or 3-s) waves as observed by MMS at the Earth’s ion foreshock region. We identified intervals of 3-s waves in each of the case studies with a strict frequency selection criteria close to ~0.3 Hz (or 3.3s). Our minimum variance analysis results indicate that these waves are nearly circularly right-handed polarized in the spacecraft frame, consistent with earlier studies. We also utilized multi-spacecraft techniques to determine an anti-sunward propagation direction of the 3-s wave in the plasma rest frame. We found that, in all of the three case studies, the 3-s waves occur sequentially with steepened and compressive 30-s waves, and can modulate or scatter the backstreaming field-aligned ion beam to form complex ion distributions in the terrestrial foreshock. Both phenomena have not been previously reported. We further investigated the instability that generates the 3-s waves based on the ion distributions associated with the observations of 3-s waves using a linear dispersion solver. We concluded that the 3-s waves play an even more important role in wave-particle interactions than previously thought, with implications in the formation and growth of other wave modes in the ion foreshock.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Observational Comparison of Large-scale Traveling Atmospheric and Ionospheric Disturbances During the May 2024 Geomagnetic Storm
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: During geomagnetic storms, Large-scale traveling atmospheric disturbances (TADs) and traveling ionospheric disturbances (TIDs) are considered to display matching propagation characteristics. However, the lack of neutral measurements has hindered a global observational comparison between TADs and TIDs. During the 10-12 May 2024 storm, with 14 satellites from Tianmu, Swarm, and GRACE-FO at around 510 km altitude, we imaged global TADs by filtering neutral density perturbations and compared them with TIDs in the form of detrended Total Electron Content (dTEC) observed by Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers across the Americas and East Asia–Australia sectors. The use of multiple satellites significantly improves longitudinal sampling and captures the spatial characteristics of TADs. At low to mid latitudes, neutral density perturbations are primarily large-scale TADs spanning about 90°–180° in longitude, while at high latitudes, they are mainly TADs extending less than 60° and stationary enhanced features. TAD wavefronts tend to align with magnetic latitude contours, likely because the magnetic field shapes their excitation source, such as the polar cusp and auroral arc. Most TADs are excited simultaneously at high latitudes on both day and night sides during rapid increases in the AE index. These features align with Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIEGCM) simulations and coincide with regions of enhanced Joule heating. By constructing keograms in two target sectors, we compared the temporal–latitudinal signatures of TADs and TIDs. Both show multiple aligned pulse trains with interference nodes at the same latitudes and comparable phase speeds estimated at 500–1100 m/s. The observed TAD trains consistently lag TID trains by about 30 minutes during propagation, likely due to the differing atmospheric gravity wave effects on neutral and plasma components, which is still an open question. In short, this work offers observational evidence of thermosphere-ionosphere wave coupling during geomagnetic storms.

presentations.presentation_title: Low-latitude Aurora and Adjacent Sub-auroral Plasma Convection During a Magnetic Storm on Jan 1, 2025
presentations.abstract: On the night of the new year day of 2025, which corresponded to the main phase of an intense magnetic storm (minimum Dst of -200 nT), continuous appearance of reddish aurora was captured by a color digital camera at Rikubetsu, Hokkaido (Glat: 43.53N, Glon: 143.61E, Mlat: 36.76N, and L-value of 1.558). During this extended interval of auroral display at mid-latitude, relatively large substorms (AE index of as large as 2000 nT) occurred three times with a separation of several hours. Following these substorm events, the aurora observed from Hokkaido got intensified, while the Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARN) radars installed in the same place simultaneously observed an increase of the plasma convection in the longitudinal direction. During these intensifications, the region of reddish auroral emission showed longitudinal drift: during the first two intensification events before midnight, the aurora moved westward, while the final intensification observed in the morning side showed eastward movement. The directions of these auroral drift well corresponded to the east-west drift velocities measured by SuperDARN. During the third intensification event, ultraviolet aurora observations by DMSP/SSUSI confirmed that the reddish aurora seen from Hokkaido had migrated southward to approximately 50 MLAT. Furthermore, the region of enhanced plasma convection observed by SuperDARN was found to be located slightly equatorward of the aurora structure. In the presentation, we will discuss the relationship between the plasma convection observed by SuperDARN and the velocities of the drifting motion of aurora, as well as the mechanism by which substorms cause intensification of mid-latitude auroras and corresponding enhancement of the background ionospheric convection.

presentations.presentation_title: Characteristics of Electron Density Variations in the Plasmasphere and Ionosphere During the May and October 2024 Super Geomagnetic Storms
presentations.abstract: In order to elucidate the temporal and spatial variation of the electron density in the plasmasphere and ionosphere during the May and October 2024 geomagnetic storms, we analyzed Global Navigation Satellite System - total electron content (TEC) and Arase satellite observation data. For identification of the electron density variation in the ionosphere, we calculated the ratio of the TEC difference (rTEC) defined as a difference from a 10 quiet-day average TEC normalized by the average value. Further, we derived the electron density in the plasmasphere and inner magnetosphere from the upper limit frequency of upper-hybrid resonance (UHR) waves observed by the Arase satellite. As a result, an L-t plot of the electron density shows a shrink of the plasmasphere from L=7.0 to L=1.5-2.5 within 10 hours after the storm onset. The severe shrinkage of the plasmasphere suggests that a strong convection electric field penetrates in the inner magnetosphere during the main phase of the geomagnetic storms. During the recovery phase of the geomagnetic storms, the plasmasphere slowly recovered the level of geomagnetically quiet periods on a 4-day scale. The time scale of the plasmaspheric refilling is much longer than that of other coronal mass ejection-driven geomagnetic storms. On the other hand, the polar maps of rTEC show that a large depletion of the rTEC value from the high to low latitudes during the recovery phase of the geomagnetic storms. The TEC depletion suggests the occurrence of a negative storm due to the neutral composition (O/N 2 ) change driven by energy input from the magnetosphere at the high-latitude thermosphere. Therefore, the contribution of a negative storm to the plasmaspheric refilling process should be taken into account in the plasmaspheric and inner magnetospheric models.

presentations.presentation_title: Strong Magnetopause Erosion During the May 2024 Solar Storm
presentations.abstract: Earth’s main magnetic field forms the magnetosphere, a barrier against solar wind plasmas. A southward magnetic field carried by the solar wind makes the magnetosphere smaller, which is termed “magnetopause erosion.” This process leads to equatorward extension of the polar region, where solar wind plasmas directly intrude into the magnetosphere. Although previous studies have suggested that magnetopause reconnection causes magnetopause erosion, the erosion mechanism during super geomagnetic storms remains controversial owing to a lack of in situ measurements. Here, we report a magnetopause crossing by the Arase satellite at 4.96 R E during the May 2024 super geomagnetic storm, which is the innermost magnetopause ever detected by magnetospheric spacecraft. An unexpected decrease in the magnetic field intensity extended from the inner magnetosphere to the magnetopause, indicating that magnetospheric currents reduced Earth’s main magnetic field on a global scale. Consequently, the solar wind pushed the weakened magnetosphere further toward the Earth, resulting in the severe shrinkage of the magnetosphere. This shrinkage led to a significant equatorward penetration of solar energetic particles in the dayside atmosphere, suggesting that the magnetospheric currents can increase the risk of aircraft exposure to solar energetic particles and shortwave radio communication disruption at mid-latitudes.

presentations.presentation_title: The Solar and Geomagnetic Storms in 2024 May: Quantifications, Contextualisations, and Updates
presentations.abstract: In May 2024, the scientific community has experienced a "perfect" solar storm. The active region 13664 quickly increased the area and trigerred 12 X-class flares and 10 halo CMEs. These solar eruptions and their combinations dramatically compressed magnetosphere, raised a ground level enhanceent (GLE), but also developped a great geomagnetic storm (minimum provisional Dst = -406 nT), intense ionospheric storm, and extended auroral ovals to the equatorward. This talk aims at reviewing what the scientific community observed for the May 2024 storm, quantifying each phenomenon, and contextualising the May 2024 storm into the extreme solar and geomagnetic storms in a longer time scale, partially on the basis of Hayakawa et al. (2025, The Astrophysical Journal, 979, 49) and the subsequent scientific developments.

This service provides registered user with access to 40 geomagnetic and solar indices. The users can view the indices in a graphical form or access the data values directly. The service is also accessible via a machine-to-machine REST interface. presentations.presentation_title: Hyper Boris Integrators for Kinetic Plasma Simulations
presentations.abstract: Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations are crucial in modern space plasma physics. In the core part of PIC simulation, the Boris method (Boris 1970; also known as the Buneman-Boris method) has been standard for more than 50 years. It is second-order accurate in time --- its numerical error is proportional to the square of the timestep, ~(Δt) 2 .In this contribution, we have substantially extended the nonrelativistic Boris solver. First, we introduce n-times subcycling: we repeat the numerical procedure n-times, with an n-times smaller timestep, Δt/n. This allows us to solve the equation with better second-order accuracy, ~(Δt/n) 2 . Second, we have introduced higher-order modification to the standard Boris method. This achieves fully higher-order accuracy, ~(Δt) N (N = 2,4,6… th order). Third, we combine these two methods to amplify their benefits. We call the new method the hyper Boris solvers, because it has two hyperparameters of the subcycling number n and the order of accuracy, N. The n-cycle Nth-order solver has an ultrahigh accuracy of ~(Δt/n) N . Computational cost of the new solver is still aﬀordable.For further details, see S. Zenitani & T. N. Kato, Comput. Phys. Commun. 315, 109695 (2025).

presentations.presentation_title: Multi-stage Resonant Particle Acceleration by Large-amplitude Alfvén Waves in a Strong Magnetic Field
presentations.abstract: Large-amplitude Alfvén waves are ubiquitous in space and astrophysical plasmas and play a fundamental role in energy transport and dissipation. We propose a novel acceleration mechanism operating in strongly magnetized plasmas, in which particles are energized through a sequence of nonlinear wave–particle interactions. Using one-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations and analytical modeling, we demonstrate that a large-amplitude Alfvén waves trigger a multi-stage acceleration process once its amplitude exceeds a critical threshold. The parent wave first excites counter-propagating daughter waves via decay instability. These waves resonantly accelerate particles perpendicular to the ambient magnetic field through counter-propagating wave–particle resonant acceleration (CWRA). The resulting increase in particle energy modifies the cyclotron frequency and induces modulational instability, generating localized electrostatic fields inside the wave packet. These fields sustain relativistic gyroresonant surfing acceleration (GRSA), during which perpendicular momentum is efficiently converted into parallel momentum through the v×B force. When the modulational field weakens, particles remain trapped by the parent wave and continue to gain energy via single-wave resonant acceleration (SWRA). In addition, the accumulation of accelerated particles self-consistently generates electrostatic trailing fields behind the wave packet, leading to trailing-field acceleration (TFA) of other particles. The combined action of CWRA, GRSA, and SWRA produces particle energies far exceeding those obtained by trailing-field acceleration alone. This multi-stage resonant process represents a fundamental plasma mechanism for converting wave energy into particle kinetic energy. The results provide new insight into wave-driven energization in heliospheric and astrophysical plasmas and offer a unified framework for understanding efficient particle acceleration by large-amplitude plasma waves.

presentations.presentation_title: An Integration-free Method to Calculate Spatial Gradients in Solar Wind Using Multi-spacecraft Data
presentations.abstract: The anomalous heating of the solar wind is widely associated with the turbulent fluctuations of the flow fields (velocity, magnetic field). Previous studies derive an exact measure of the turbulent heating rate of the solar wind using incompressible MHD formalism, with an assumption of isotropy. However, due to the non-negligible mean magnetic field, the anisotropy in the energy transfer cannot be ignored. An alternative exact law has been recently derived by Banerjee and Galtier (JoPA, 2017) without making the assumption of isotropy but requires knowledge of the curls of flow fields. Several methods to calculate curls using multi-spacecraft data have been proposed based on vector integration theorems, Curlometer being the most popular. They provide an average value of the curl for the whole multi-spacecraft system (tetrahedron for Cluster and MMS). We propose an integration-free method (IFM) based on the construction of an orthonormal coordinate system fixed to the spacecraft for the calculation of spatial derivatives at the position of each spacecraft (Singh et al, 2026, submitted to A&A). Using a total of 107 datasets from MMS (NASA) between 2015 and 2017, we calculate the point-wise curls of magnetic field (current density) and ion fluid velocity (vorticity). We compare the average values of the curls calculated using IFM with those using Curlometer which show an excellent agreement with a correlation coefficient of nearly 0.99 between them. We show that the quality of the curl improves with the regularity of the tetrahedron. Unlike the other methods, IFM can also be applied to three-spacecraft systems. This method is particularly useful for calculating the energy cascade rate in the solar wind.

presentations.presentation_title: Lu and Hamilton Model for Solar Flares Over a Rewiring Complex Network
presentations.abstract: We present a modified Lu & Hamilton–type model where the neighborhood relations are replaced by topological connections, which can be dynamically altered. The model represents each grid node as a flux tube, as in the classic model, but with connections evolving to capture the complex effects of magnetic reconnection. Through this framework, we analyze how the dissipated energy distribution changes, particularly focusing on the power-law exponent α E , which decreases with respect to the original model due to rewiring effects. When the system is dominated by rewiring, it presents an exponential distribution exponent β E , showing a faster decay of dissipated energy than in the original model. This leads to microflare-dominated dynamics at short timescales, causing the system to lose the scale-free behavior observed in both the original model and in configurations where energy release is primarily driven by forcing rather than rewiring. Our results reveal a clear transition from power-law to exponential regimes as the rewiring probability increases, fundamentally altering the energy distribution characteristics of the system. In contrast, when considering topological neighbors instead of local ones, the model’s dynamics become intrinsically nonlocal. This leads to scaling exponents comparable to those reported in other nonlocal dynamical systems.

presentations.presentation_title: Activity and Cumulative Entropy in Mhd Simulations Via the Goy Shell Model with Fractal Forcing
presentations.abstract: In the study of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), one of the proposed models is the GOY Shell Model, which solves the usual MHD equations via coupled shells in the Fourier space for the velocity and magnetic field of the fluid, correctly reproducing nonlinear effects and statistical properties of turbulence such as power-law distribution of dissipative events. Previous studies performed with this model showed a relation between the fractal dimension of the magnetic dissipation and activity parameters of the time series with a Langevin-type forcing. In this work, we seek to study if the Cumulative Entropy, proposed as an alternative to Shannon Entropy, shows a correlation with any of the activity parameters proposed in the literature and the effect of varying the fractal dimension of the forcing. For this, we solved the GOY Shell Model equations under different types of forcing in the velocity and magnetic field. The forcings used were antipersistent Fractional Brownian Motion (FBM) time series, in at least one of the dynamic fields (velocity or magnetic field), and Langevin or Gaussian noise in the other. After this, we calculated the time series of the system’s magnetic dissipation rate, studied its cumulative entropy for sliding windows along the time series, and calculated the cumulative entropy of the whole time series. We have compared the cumulative entropy of the whole series with four activity parameters previously used in the literature. Early results show that for three of the five types of simulations, the cumulative entropy is well correlated with the average magnetic dissipation.

presentations.presentation_title: First Results of the Interstellar Dust Experiment Onboard NASA's IMAP Mission
presentations.abstract: Since January 2026, NASA’s Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe (IMAP) has been operating at the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point to investigate how the heliosphere interacts with its interstellar environment. IMAP carries a suite of ten instruments—combining in situ and remote-sensing capabilities—to address fundamental questions about the local interstellar medium (LISM), the heliosphere’s boundary regions, and the sources and transport of energetic particles. Among these instruments is the Interstellar Dust Experiment (IDEX), designed to characterize the flux, size distribution, chemical, elemental, and isotopic composition of dust particles entering the Solar System from the LISM. These interstellar dust (ISD) grains are direct physical samples of contemporary interstellar solid matter, providing insight into the composition of the local interstellar cloud. A key objective of IDEX is to assess whether the current dust population in the LISM is compositionally consistent with the primordial material from which the Solar System formed. IDEX will also test models of dust propagation through the heliosphere, including how magnetic fields and solar activity filter small charged grains. These measurements will contribute to developing improved models of the heliospheric boundary and the processes that govern dust entry into the inner heliosphere. IDEX is an impact ionization mass spectrometer, wherein high-velocity dust particles striking a target surface produce ions that are analyzed in a time-of-flight (TOF) setup. This presentation will provide an overview of IDEX’s scientific objectives, measurement capabilities, and expected contributions to heliophysics and planetary science. Preliminary performance data and early results will also be discussed, highlighting IDEX’s role in advancing our understanding of the physical link between interstellar and solar system materials.

presentations.presentation_title: MAGDAS：The Global Geomagnetic Observation Network, and Its Applications in Space Weather
presentations.abstract: Kyushu University has been continuously operating a global geomagnetic observation network for more than forty years since the 1980s. At present, these activities are carried out within MAGDAS (MAGnetic Data Acquisition System) project, operated by the International Research Center for Space and Planetary Environmental Science (i-SPES). One of the features of MAGDAS project is its unique configuration, consisting of a meridional chain aligned along the geomagnetic longitude of approximately 210 degrees, including Japan, and an zonal chain along the geomagnetic equator. This configuration enables us to capture, with high temporal resolution, both the detailed propagation of magnetic field disturbances from high latitudes to the equatorial region and the global state of geomagnetic variations in the magnetic equatorial zone. The observations are conducted using ground-based fluxgate magnetometers, in addition to other instruments, such as induction magnetometers, FM-CW radars, and software radio based ionospheric scintillation detectors.Using high-quality data obtained from this observation network, numerous scientific results have been produced in the fields of magnetosphere–ionosphere coupling, including studies of ULF waves, Sq variations, Equatorial Electrojet, etc. To elucidate the physical processes in the magnetic equatorial region, a novel geomagnetic index, the EE-index, was developed to monitor both short- and long-term variations of the equatorial electrojet current.The geomagnetic data and related index products maintained by the project team members are publicly available, not only through our project website, but also via inter-university collaborative project called IUGONET and University Institutional Repository. These data dissemination activities are conducted in accordance with the FAIR principles, ensuring appropriate open-access and reusability.MAGDAS project is founded on numerous international partnerships, where the project activities are maintained through sustainable cooperative relationships with researchers worldwide. Such cooperative relationships include joint research programs, on-site capacity-building at observation stations, and the return of outcomes via data DOIs.

presentations.presentation_title: Generation of Quasi‐periodic Dayside Medium Scale Traveling Ionospheric Disturbances(mstids) by Intermittent Lobe Reconnection
presentations.abstract: The medium scale traveling ionospheric disturbances(MSTIDs) can be excited by many sources. Among those magnetic reconnection has been proposed as a potential driver for dayside MSTIDs, but direct evidence has been limited. Using ground based radar data from the SuperDual on 14 December 2012, we observed quasiperiodic multiple MSTIDs propagating from auroral latitudes to midlatitudes near magnetic local noon,which showed one‐to‐one correspondence sto intermittent lobereconnections with periodicities of about 20-30min. Simultaneous EISCAT Svalbard incoherent scatter radar data revealed enhanced electric field and Joule heating within the cusp region following each lobe reconnection. Thesemulti instrument observations strongly suggest lobe reconnection as a possible driver for the dayside MSTID.

presentations.presentation_title: Recent Commissioning Progress on the CMP-IPS Radio Telescope Array in Northern China
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: Interplanetary scintillation (IPS) phenomenon behaves as twinkling of a compact radio source due to scattering in the solar wind. The scattering and scintillation of emergent radio waves are ascribed to turbulent density irregularities transported by the ubiquitous solar wind. The bulk-flow speed and turbulent spectrum of the solar wind streams can be extracted from the single-station power spectra fitting and the multi-station cross-correlation analysis. A new three-site IPS-dedicated facility in northern China was constructed in early 2025 within the Meridian-II Space Weather Monitoring Project. In this talk, we will present the recent progress on the raw data calibration and its relevant numerical magnetohydrodynamic model during the ongoing commissioning phase of our CMP-IPS telescopes.

presentations.presentation_title: Global Spatial Distribution of Pi 2 Geomagnetic Pulsations: a Detailed Analysis of the Day–night Terminator Region
presentations.abstract: Pi 2 geomagnetic pulsations are transient oscillations with periods of 40–150 seconds that originate mainly in the nightside magnetosphere and are observed globally during substorm onset. Clarifying their spatiotemporal distribution and propagation characteristics is important for understanding the magnetosphere–ionosphere (M–I) coupling system. This study aims to elucidate the spatiotemporal characteristics of Pi 2 pulsations and clarify the global M–I coupling at substorm onset.In previous studies, our group has analyzed data observed by the MAGDAS magnetometer network along the 210° magnetic meridian chain and in the North and South American chain. These studies suggested that nightside Pi 2 pulsations are caused by fast-mode waves or the Biot–Savart component of substorm current wedge (SCW) oscillations [Uozumi et al., 2009], dayside Pi 2 pulsations are driven by ionospheric currents, and dawn-side Pi 2 pulsations are associated with terminator currents [Imajo et al., 2015]. In contrast, dusk Pi 2 pulsations exhibit more complicated spatial characteristics, and their underlying sources remain poorly understood.In this study, the spatial distribution of dusk-side Pi 2 pulsations during the local E-layer sunset, taken from the MAGDAS dataset, were analyzed. The results show that the events can be broadly classified according to the local time at each station (daytime, nighttime, and dusk); however, some events did not fit the existing classification scheme.As a case study, we considered an event wherein two mid-latitude stations in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres were located in the daytime region. We identified enhanced amplitudes and phase shifts in the northward H and eastward D components. Further analysis revealed a component distinct from the nightside contribution, likely from an ionospheric current reflecting the Cowling effect flowing along the terminator [Yoshikawa, 2012]. Future work will focus on analyzing further similar events and integrating other data sources.

presentations.presentation_title: A Statistical Study of Polar Cap Patch Occurrence and IMF Dependence Using GNSS TEC Maps
presentations.abstract: We present an automated algorithm for identifying the two-dimensional distribution of polar cap patches from GNSS Total Electron Content (TEC) maps, combining dynamic thresholding with a set of physical constraints. The performance of the algorithm is validated using a well-documented event, showing close agreement with manual identification in both timing and spatial morphology. Using GNSS TEC data from 2020 to 2024, we analyze the seasonal, Universal Time (UT), and Interplanetary Magnetic Field (IMF) dependencies of patch occurrence in the northern polar cap. The resulting patterns are generally consistent with previous studies, with results from solar-maximum years appearing more reliable. Focusing on the solar-maximum year 2023, we further examine the relationship between patch formation and preceding IMF variations. The statistical analysis reveals that both rapid changes and large-amplitude variations in IMF By and Bz are closely associated with patch formation, with these IMF fluctuations typically preceding patch formation by about 10–15 minutes. This suggests that IMF-driven modulation of the ionospheric convection pattern plays an important role in polar cap patch formation. These results provide new statistical evidence linking IMF variations to patch formation and demonstrate the capability of TEC-based methods for statistical patch studies.

presentations.presentation_title: Multiple Auroral Arcs Propagating Tailward Under Northward IMF
presentations.abstract: We present observations of recurrent tailward-propagating auroral arcs in the dawnside during a period of northward IMF. THEMIS satellites located near the dawnside magnetopause in the equatorial plane observed strong fluctuations in magnetic field and ion bulk velocity with periods of 5–10 minutes, suggesting the presence of surface waves or ULF waves. This was followed by shorter-period fluctuations of 2–3 minutes in both magnetic field and plasma parameters for an hour, indicating the development of Kelvin–Helmholtz instability (KHI). During these wave intervals, a ground-based all-sky imager detected recurrent auroral arcs detached from the poleward boundary of the auroral oval, propagating predominantly tailward. DMSP observations revealed multiple auroral arcs on the dawnside, accompanied by electron precipitation associated with paired upward and downward field-aligned currents. Based on these coordinated space- and ground-based observations, we discuss several possible generation mechanisms for the observed auroral arcs, including surface waves, ULF waves, and KHI.

presentations.presentation_title: Polar Ionospheric Electric Current System Deduced from Data Assimilation Into an Emulator of a Magnetosphere-ionosphere Model
presentations.abstract: The modelling of the ionospheric electric currents is important for discussing the geomagnetic variations at high latitudes. We have recently developed a data assimilation system which incorporates ground-based observations such as SuperDARN radar data into an emulator of a global magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model of the magnetosphere. This system conducts data assimilation with an algorithm based on the ensemble transform Kalman filter to estimate the electric potential distribution in the polar ionosphere. In this study, we calculated the ionospheric current distribution from the potential distribution estimated with the data assimilation system. The field-aligned currents (FACs) were then obtained from the ionospheric current distribution. The results successfully reproduced large-scale features of the ionospheric currents and FACs. We will discuss the temporal variations of the polar ionospheric current system derived from the potential distribution obtained by the data assimilation.

presentations.presentation_title: Effects of Future Co2 Levels on Ionospheric Electron Density Response to Geomagnetic Storms
presentations.abstract: This work investigates how ionospheric electron density responds to geomagnetic storms under increasing greenhouse gas levels using the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model with thermosphere-ionosphere eXtension (WACCM-X). May 2024-like geomagnetic storms are simulated for four years (2016, 2040, 2061, and 2084) corresponding to CO₂ concentrations of 403, 500, 652, and 918 ppmv, following the “worst-case” projections given by the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6, Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5. Our results indicate that higher CO₂ levels weaken the ionospheric response to geomagnetic storms. The peak electron density in the F2 layer (NmF2) declines markedly at midlatitudes, while showing modest increases in auroral and equatorial regions, with hemispheric asymmetry. The largest reductions occur between 220 and 400 km altitude.

presentations.presentation_title: Solar Wind–driven Global Fast Magnetosonic Waves in the Magnetosphere
presentations.institution: Institute of Solar-Terrestrial Physics SB RAS
presentations.abstract: A prolonged Pc5 wave event was observed on the dayside of the magnetosphere on 15 February 2014 by the Van Allen Probes A and B and the THEMIS-E spacecraft. The total duration of the observed wave activity exceeded 8 hours. The wave frequency varied between 1 and 3.5 mHz, with peak magnetic field amplitudes reaching up to 5 nT.It was found that the plasma pressure and parallel component of the wave magnetic field oscillate in phase, indicating fast magnetosonic nature of the observed waves. The beginning of the wave activity was associated with the arrival of an interplanetary shock to the magnetosphere. The subsequent oscillations were driven by sharp changes in the solar wind dynamic pressure.Simultaneously, geomagnetic pulsations within the same frequency band were recorded by numerous high-latitude ground-based magnetometers in the Northern Hemisphere. The pulsations were detected across several meridian chains of magnetometers, demonstrating the longitudinally large-scale spatial extent of the event. Phase relationships between magnetic field oscillations at closely spaced stations were analyzed, revealing signatures of the field line resonance. The azimuthal wave numbers range from m = 0 to m = 5. That is, the pulsations observed on the ground are caused by azimuthally large-scale Alfven waves excited in the magnetosphere by the observed fast magnetosonic waves.This work was supported by the Russian Science Foundation (project No. 24-77-10012).

presentations.presentation_title: Long-duration Pseudobreakups
presentations.institution: Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute
presentations.abstract: Pseudobreakups (pseudosubstorms) are generally believed to be weaker, more localized, and more short-lived than substorms, but are similar to substorms, particularly the early stage of the substorm expansion phase. Previous studies defined the pseudobreakup by small latitudinal extent or short duration of auroral onset arc activity or poleward expansion. A distinct morphological difference, however, appears to be auroral poleward expansion or auroral breakup. While substorm auroral onset arcs develop into poleward expansion, pseudobreakups subside without progressing to poleward expansion. Here, using Time History of Events and Macroscale Interactions during Substorms (THEMIS) data, we show pseudobreakup events that lasted more than 10 min. They had a latitudinal extent of less than ~3 degrees and were morphologically similar to usual short-lived pseudobreakups. Although the latitudinal extent may work to some extent to define the pseudobreakup, the duration does not seem to work. We suggest that the pseudobreakup should be defined morphologically by poleward expansion.

Direct Observation of Ion-electron Decoupling in Magnetic Reconnection
presentations.abstract: Ion-electron decoupling at ion scale lead to Hall effect, the indicative process of collisionless magnetic reconnection. Past observations have revealed the features of Hall current system in L direction, Hall magnetic field in M direction and Hall electric field in N direction. However until now, there is no observations on the ion-electron decoupling（Hall current）in N direction, where Hall effect originates. In this study, using MMS observation, we find ion-electron decoupling（Hall current）in N direction in the separatrix region at the magnetospheric side of a reconnection current sheet. A comprehensive analysis provides the insight to the process of ion-electron decoupling, regarding electron motion, composition of Hall electron, and charge distribution. From micro mechanism, the results deep our understanding of solar wind-magnetosphere coupling triggered by reconnection, and support the upcoming study based the observation from launched SMILE mission.

presentations.presentation_title: High-energy Electron Enhancements Deep Inside the Plasmasphere Driven by Fast Solar Wind
presentations.institution: National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: The Earth's outer radiation contains plenty of high-energy electrons. These electron populations exhibit high dynamics, with their fluxes varying by several orders of magnitude. The enhancement of these high-energy electrons greatly increases the likelihood of spacecraft malfunction or failure and significantly influences the solar-terrestrial system's energy and mass coupling, highlighting the importance of fully understanding the mechanisms governing these dynamics from both theoretical and practical perspectives. The plasmasphere is a region usually associated with high-energy electron loss. Using Van Allen Probes measurements, we have found rapid, multi-MeV electron enhancements deep inside the plasmasphere (RMEEIP) that developed within hours at low L-shells, which is distinct from the prompt shock-induced enhancement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this RMEEIP is closely associated with the penetration of intense convection electric field inside plasmasphere (PCEF) induced by the high-speed solar wind. This study provides direct evidence that RMEEIP are closely connected to PCEF. The research results are helpful for deepening the understanding of the formation and evolution of high-energy electrons in the radiation belt.

presentations.presentation_title: Extreme O⁺ Enrichment In The Deep Inner Magnetosphere During Severe Geomagnetic Storms
presentations.abstract: During the super geomagnetic storm of 10–11 May 2024, an extreme enhancement in plasma mass density was observed at L~2.5. Multi-point ground magnetometer observations revealed that this enhancement extended over a wide longitudinal range—from New Zealand through Europe to eastern North America—during the storm’s main and early recovery phases. The maximum density, approximately 35,000 amu/cm 3 , was detected in the New Zealand longitude sector. In this study, we employ an integrated analysis combining ground magnetometer measurements, Arase and DMSP satellite data, and GNSS-based TEC maps to investigate the highly O + -rich state and the enhancement of plasma mass density in the inner magnetosphere. Ground-based magnetometer data provide the global distribution of field line resonance (FLR) signatures and enable estimation of plasma mass density at the equatorial crossing points of individual magnetic field lines. Arase observations of plasma wave spectra and energetic particles allow derivation of local plasma densities and particle energy distributions, while DMSP and GNSS-derived TEC maps provide complementary ionospheric context. Plasmaspheric electron densities derived from Arase plasma wave measurements indicate in situ electron densities of approximately 1,500 /cm 3 at L~2.5. Combined with mass density estimates, the inferred ion composition suggests a dominance of heavy ions, with O + fractions exceeding 90%. The coexistence of cold and warm plasma populations, elevated ionospheric electron temperatures, and significant TEC depletions over New Zealand and its conjugate point indicate heating of cold electrons through Coulomb collisions with warm ions, followed by strong heating of ionospheric electrons and subsequent heavy ion upflow. In addition, geomagnetic data during the intense storm of 10 October 2024 (Dst minimum −333 nT) reveal clear FLR signatures indicating enhanced plasma mass density at similar L-shells, suggesting that such mass loading is not unique to the May 2024 superstorm.

presentations.presentation_title: Magnetosheath Jets and Their Soft X-ray Imaging by a Virtual Telescope: Parametric Study
presentations.institution: Institute of Space Science - INFLPR Subsidiary
presentations.abstract: This work is focused on assessing the observational thresholds of high-speed magnetosheath jets by a virtual soft X-ray telescope using numerical simulations. For this purpose, we performed a parametric study to investigate the impact of plasma density and bulk velocity on the soft X-ray imaging of jets for different setups of the X-ray telescope. In our simulations, the high‐speed plasma jets are defined as local perturbations of the background density and bulk velocity. The background plasma is simulated globally with a three-dimensional MHD code of the Earth’s magnetosphere, while the jet is propagated kinematically in the magnetosheath. The soft X‐ray emissivity is computed from a fluid‐like model of the solar wind charge exchange process. A virtual telescope placed inside the simulation domain provides line-of-sight and time integrated images of the X-ray volume emission rate. Our results show that the denser high‐speed plasma jets are more likely to be detected by a soft X‐ray telescope than the faster jets. Also, the soft X‐ray detection of jets is substantially enhanced when the telescope is located in the equatorial plane, pointing toward the magnetotail. We discuss the potential implications of our simulations for SMILE-SXI. Starting from 2026, SMILE (Solar wind-Magnetosphere-Ionosphere Link Explorer), a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Chinese Academy of Science, shall observe in-situ and remotely (in soft X-rays and UV) the interaction between the solar wind plasma and the terrestrial magnetosphere.

presentations.presentation_title: Instrumentation For In Situ Measurements of Thermospheric Winds
presentations.abstract: A program in developing instrumentation for making in situ neutral gas measurements in the upper atmosphere is described. The measurements focus on winds, but also include density and temperature. Current designs are presented and discussed, including those tailored for sounding rockets, cubesats, and traditional satellites. The new Thermo series of sensors for use on cubesats is described. Also discussed is a novel instrument that measures cross-track winds and temperature using an imaging technique that requires no moving elements. Recent results from lab testing and sounding rocket flights are presented.

presentations.presentation_title: Hybrid Fluxgate/Search-Coil Magnetometer Microdevice
presentations.abstract: To better understand the forces acting on objects in space, researchers use fluxgate and search-coil magnetometers to measure the Earth’s magnetic field and electromagnetic waves generated by the sun. The last decade has seen the creation of a combined fluxgate/search-coil magnetometer as well as the chip size satellite (chip-sat). These advancements have led to the need for a hybrid fluxgate/search-coil magnetometer microdevice that can be launched in tandem with the chip-sat payload. This microdevice is achievable using the design breakthroughs previously mentioned along with a novel material science approach for fabrication of the magnetic core. The project is just entering its design phase and has already undergone parametric evaluation and logistical analysis.The material science of the magnetic cores for the fluxgate magnetometers used in a majority of space missions has been almost completely reliant on a single batch of 6-81 Permalloy for the last 50 plus years. While this yields considerable result consistency and data science integration efficiency, it is size prohibitive for any future missions involving chip-sat payloads. It is therefore necessary to utilize adjacent material science improvements from the inductor core sector to create a high permeability amorphous alloy for measuring from DC to kHz frequencies. The Phase 1 target of a 10 cm by 10 cm test vehicle for confirming the experimental magnetic core performance against existing materials, including 6-81 Permalloy, is currently underway. Validation of material properties and improved chip fabrication techniques will lead to Phase 2 where a 2 cm by 2 cm prototype will be tested terrestrially in vacuum chamber and anechoic electromagnetic isolation chamber. Additional testing aboard a rocket to confirm in-space functionality of the device and sensitivity of the sensors is expected in the near future.

presentations.presentation_title: The High Energy Proton SSD Telescope and ChErenkov Radiator (HEPSTER): Extending Capabilities of the MERiT (Miniaturized Electron pRoton Telescope)
presentations.abstract: The High Energy Proton SSD Telescope and chErenkov Radiator (HEPSTER) is a space weather instrument capable of measuring solar energetic particles (SEPs) in the unique energy range of ~10 – 500 MeV. HEPSTER extends the capabilities of the MERiT instrument, a traditional SSD-only particle telescope, also developed at Goddard. High-energy charged particles in the form of episodic solar energetic particles (SEPs) represent one of the most significant space weather (SWx) hazards both for human space flight and space assets, therefore fully characterizing these particles is critical. Currently, there is a lack of high-energy SEP proton measurements in the Heliophysics Systems Observatory (HSO). The HEPSTER instrument will bridge this measurement gap utilizing a unique combination of both solid-state detectors (SSDs) and Cherenkov detectors optimized for the environment. HEPSTER is much more compact than prior designs, ideal for modern launch opportunities. We will provide a brief overview of MERiT, highlighting enhancements provided by HEPSTER. We will also describe the unique challenges in integrating signals from two different detector types, namely, SSDs and Cherenkov radiators.

presentations.presentation_title: The Tandem Reconnection and Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites (TRACERS) - Mission Design and First Results
presentations.abstract: The overarching science goal of the Tandem Reconnection And Cusp Electrodynamics Reconnaissance Satellites (TRACERS) mission is to connect the cusp to the magnetosphere by discovering how spatial or temporal variations in magnetic reconnection drive cusp dynamics. This goal isachieved with a simple mission design comprising two identical small spacecraft in identical low-Earth orbits in a follow-the-leader configuration. TRACERS makes repeated measurements in the cusp for a twelve-month primary mission using plasma and field instruments. These data are analyzed using established dual-spacecraft techniques and supported by modeling that ensures science closure on the objectives. The TRACERS team leverages hardware collaborations from the University of Iowa, Southwest Research Institute, University of California Los Angeles, University of California Berkeley, and Millennium Space Systems. The larger science team consists of experts in reconnection, cusp physics, and modeling. TRACERS is dedicated to its proposer, and original Principal Investigator, Professor Craig Kletzing.

presentations.presentation_title: Auroral Imaging on the NASA’s New Small Explorer Mission – the Cross-scale Investigation of Earth’s Magnetotail and Aurora (CINEMA)
presentations.abstract: The Cross-Scale INvestigation of Earth’s Magnetotail and Aurora (CINEMA) is NASA’s Small Explorer mission recently selected for Phase B, currently targeting launch no sooner than 2030. CINEMA is a nine spacecraft constellation designed to investigate the role of plasma sheet structure and evolution in Earth’s multiscale magnetospheric convection cycle. CINEMA will investigate how the plasma sheet sustains steady magnetospheric convection, what controls the onset of explosive energy release in the magnetotail, and how plasma sheet structure and kinetic-scale particle precipitation are linked to mesoscale auroral dynamics. For the first time, CINEMA combines comprehensive energetic particle detectors, magnetometers, and Auroral IMagers (AIM) that will provide wide field-of-view auroral images on each spacecraft in the constellation. To capture magnetospheric dynamics across a wide range of temporal and spatial scales, CINEMA will initially operate in a meridional string-of-pearls configuration, covering 96° in latitude, with adjacent spacecraft separated by approximately 3 minutes. This configuration allows tracking of rapidly evolving events. Later in the mission, the constellation will be reconfigured into three orbital planes spanning a broad range of longitudes for studies of longitudinal spatial evolution. AIM provides a field of view covering more than 500 km in each dimension, with a maximum cadence of 0.5 s per frame. These capabilities enable identification of large-scale substorm expansions and mesoscale auroral features, including auroral beads, poleward boundary intensifications, and streamers. The temporal variability of these mesoscale aurora spans a wide range, requiring AIM to generate simultaneous image products at multiple cadences and exposure times. This is achieved by co-adding images over 3 s and 10 s intervals, respectively. With sufficient image quality, AIM is designed to identify a wide range of auroral forms, providing data products that will not only toward the science objectives of the CINEMA but also benefit the broader space physics community.

presentations.presentation_title: Solid State Detector (SSD) Instrumentation for In-situ High Energy Particle Detection: MERIT on HERMES and AGILE on Gensat-1
presentations.abstract: Characterization of charged particles are critical to the quantitative understanding of the physics of energization, transport and loss of charged particles throughout the heliosphere. This characterization implies measuring particle intensities, spectra, and pitch angle, and identification of particle species. Solid state detector based particle telescopes have been used in many missions from Voyager to Van Allen Probes. I describe two instruments: (i) the Miniaturized Electron pRoton ion Telescope, MERIT, a classic particle telescope, for The Heliophysics Environmental and Radiation Measurement Experiment Suite, HERMES, slated to fly on ARTEMIS, Lunar gateway (ii) the Advanced enerGetic Ion eLectron tElescope,AGILE), the science payload on GenSat-1 CubeSat. Both the instruments have been built, tested, calibrated and delivered. HERMES will operate in a cis-lunar orbit in interplanetary space and GenSat-1 is expected to be launched in the autumn of 2026 into a high inclination low earth orbit. MERIT is based on a classic dE/E approach and AGILE utilizes for the first time in space, full pulse shape discrimination, PSD, to identify and characterize solar energetic particles (SEP). PSD measures the pulse shape within a single SSD using a state-of-art sampling ASIC with pico second time resolution, developed for high energy physics applications.

presentations.presentation_title: Gnss Positioning Resilience to Ionospheric Scintillation: Mitigation and Quality Control
presentations.abstract: Ionospheric scintillation is a rapid fluctuation of radio‑signal amplitude and phase caused by small‑scale irregularities in ionospheric electron density. They induce fast temporal and spatial variations that can severely degrade transionospheric signals. For GNSS receivers, scintillation appears as deep fades in carrier‑to‑noise ratio (C/N0), increased phase and range noise, frequent cycle slips, and occasional loss of lock on one or more frequencies — with consequences for positioning accuracy, timing, and integrity. Parameters such as S4 and sigma‑phi characterize the amplitude and phase scintillation levels but are not, by themselves, quality‑control (QC) metrics for positioning solutions. QC metrics assess the internal consistency and reliability of the estimation process under disturbed conditions. Key QC indicators to report alongside positioning results include: residual statistics and chi‑square tests to check that residuals match assumed noise models; formal uncertainties (covariance matrix) and RMS of position errors to compare predicted vs. observed precision; ambiguity‑resolution diagnostics: fix rate, false‑fix rate, and ratio‑test distributions showing the robustness of integer fixing; cycle‑slip counts and loss‑of‑lock events as practical integrity indicators; C/N0 distributions as receiver‑level observables linked to tracking quality. In this presentation, by processing data from a setup designed to simulate GBAS operational scenario in Brazil, in which receivers were adjusted to output raw intensity and phase data at 50 Hz and observables at 2 Hz, we will: (a) summarize the physical mechanisms and signatures of scintillation; (b) describe mitigation strategies (multi‑frequency/multi‑constellation processing, adaptive weighting, and model‑based corrections); and (c) present a comprehensive QC report — chi‑square outcomes, formal versus empirical errors, ambiguity‑resolution statistics, cycle‑slip statistics, and C/N0 — to demonstrate not only reduced positioning errors but also preserved estimator integrity and operational readiness under scintillation conditions.

presentations.presentation_title: Study on Autonomous Navigation Via Inter-satellite Links Between Gnss and Cislunar/ Lunar-orbiting Satellites
presentations.institution: Shanghai Astronomical Observatory, Chinese Academy of Sciences
presentations.abstract: At present, the high-precision ranging technology based on inter-satellite Ka-band links has achieved a breakthrough at the 100,000 km level. The integration of this technology with the GNSS constellation provides a spatial datum for satellites operating in typical orbits of the cislunar space (including DRO, NRHO and lunar orbits), emerging as a new approach to enhance the navigation capability for cislunar and deep space exploration missions. In this paper, three cislunar and lunar orbital constellations are designed, and the inter-satellite link observation data between GNSS satellites (MEO/GEO/ISGO) and cislunar satellites in three typical orbital types , such as DRO (Distant Retrograde Orbit), NRHO (Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit), and satellites at cislunar triangular and collinear libration points) are simulated. Under the chaotic orbital dynamic conditions of a hybrid two-body and three-body system, the autonomous navigation accuracy using inter-satellite links is analyzed for two operational modes—GNSS satellites participating in orbital parameters solution and GNSS satellites serving as a fixed datum without participating in orbital solution—in combination with different types of GNSS satellites. The results demonstrate that GNSS satellites can significantly accelerate the convergence speed of orbit determination for cislunar satellites and improve the orbit determination performance of cislunar vehicles to the 10-meter even meter level. These findings indicate that the integration of GNSS satellites and inter-satellite link technology serves as a powerful supplement to ground-based TT&C (Tracking, Telemetry and Command) resources, laying a solid foundation for establishing deep space navigation system for deep space exploration and enabling precise navigation services for interstellar space probes in the future.

presentations.presentation_title: Topographically Informed Regression for InSAR Tropospheric Correction: Taiwan Tropospheric Delay Model
presentations.abstract: While differential interferometry synthetic aperture radar (DInSAR) is an efficient technique in deformation monitoring, the accuracy of DInSAR measurement is often jeopardized by tropospheric delay due to spatial-temporal variation of weather conditions. Especially in tropical-subtropical regions like Taiwan, humid climate and complex topography limit the effectiveness of popular correction methods like those using numerical weather models. Taiwan’s dense continuous GNSS network provides an opportunity to develop a localized Taiwan Tropospheric Delay (TTD) model for DInSAR tropospheric correction. For this purpose, we compute zenith total delay (ZTD) data from more than 400 GNSS stations using GispyX software and Vienna Mapping Function. We then apply Topographically InformEd Regression model (TIER) to obtain the spatially-varying transfer function between delay and elevation. For each grid where the transfer function is to be estimated, we adopt a station-selection strategy that accounts for uneven distribution of GNSS stations. Weights are assigned to the selected stations based on the distance from the grid to the stations, elevation differences between the grid and the stations, distance to coast, and the sparsity of stations. The transfer function at each grid is then estimated with a weighted least-square regression. The final ZTD map is estimated using the spatially filtered transfer function map. To evaluate the performance of TTD model, we generate 184 interferograms paired from 60 ALOS-2/PALSAR-2 ScanSAR acquisitions. The displacements are corrected using tropospheric delays derived from the TTD model and ERA5. The correction using TTD model shows an average reduction in displacement standard deviation of 8% compared to the correction done using ERA-5 model, with the maximum reduction as much as 45%.

presentations.presentation_title: GNSS Remote Sensing Multi-source Troposphere Observing Technique
presentations.institution: Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences
presentations.abstract: Accurate monitoring of tropospheric water vapor is fundamental for numerical weather prediction, climate analysis, and severe weather detection. Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) remote sensing has emerged as a key observing technique, providing continuous, all-weather measurements with high temporal resolution. This study presents an integrated multi-source tropospheric observing framework that exploits complementary GNSS sensing techniques, including ground-based GNSS (fixed and mobile receivers), GNSS Radio Occultation (GNSS-RO), and GNSS Reflectometry (GNSS-R), within an unified approach. The framework propose use of ground-based GNSS observations to estimate slant tropospheric delays through multi-GNSS precise positioning, combined with excess phase observations derived from GNSS-RO and phase delay from GNSS-R over ocean surfaces. The integration of space-borne and ground-based GNSS data enhances both the vertical resolution and horizontal coverage of the reconstructed water vapor fields. Advanced tomographic inversion strategies incorporating physical and stochastic constraints are applied to mitigate the ill-posed nature of tropospheric reconstruction. Additional background information from numerical weather prediction models is introduced as weak constraints to stabilize the solution while preserving observation-driven variability. The proposed multi-source fusion framework improves the representation of rapidly evolving tropospheric structures, particularly during convective and frontal events. Results indicate that the integrated GNSS tomography approach yields more accurate and physically consistent water vapor distributions than single-technique GNSS solutions. Improvements are most pronounced in the middle and lower troposphere, where traditional GNSS observations alone are limited in vertical sensitivity. This study highlights the role of GNSS as a comprehensive remote sensing system for tropospheric observation as a driver for physical and AI weather forecasting.
